Since a person who is in a certain state is very likely to find it difficult to be patient with another, He, the Exalted, said, encouraging and warning: ﴿And know that Allah﴾, meaning: the One who possesses all greatness, ﴿intervenes﴾, meaning: by the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the perfection of His power, ﴿between a man and his heart﴾, so He turns it back to what He knows of it, and so it becomes, in what the state reveals, a disbelieving obstinate one, after having been, outwardly, a believer and submissive. Thus he will be among those whom Allah knows to have no good in them, and He has compelled them to respond, but they do not persist in it. And He returns the disbeliever, after his obstinacy, to faith, to the utmost of what He sees of ease in leading him. Glorified is He, by the intense nearness that necessarily entails intervening, He alluded to the intensity of His power to change resolutions and desires. This is an exhortation to hasten to follow the Messenger (ﷺ) while hearts are turned toward that, out of fear of their changing.

Since He warned them of the consequence of the present state, He cautioned them about the matter of the final outcome, saying: ﴿And that He﴾, meaning: and know that He, the Exalted, ﴿to Him you will be gathered﴾, not to anyone else. He will gather those who responded among the group of believers, and those who turned away among the ranks of the disbelievers, even if they refuse one ruling, because religion cannot be divided. It is known that *idha* (when) is not a condition; rather, it is an alert to the obligation of following him in everything he calls to, because of his infallibility. The wisdom of using it is to inform that he left no good unless he called to it. Al-Harrali said at the end of a book of his on the foundations of jurisprudence: "Infallibility (*'isma*) has two meanings. The first is the infallibility of preservation, which is a meaning arising from the obligation of the ruling upon him by the past of his law. This is the general infallibility of the prophets, and at this level discussion takes place about preservation from minor sins, after agreement on preservation from what would spoil the conveyance and lower the rank, and from major sins. The reality of minor sins is the preliminary steps of sins that were not completed, so that their completion would make them major. On this basis, some people built the possibility of a forbidden act occurring from a prophet. All of that, though it is among the states of prophets, the established matter concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) is only that he is exalted above this station.

The second meaning of infallibility is the lifting of the ruling from the Prophet (ﷺ) by what the preserver has preserved of the past of the apparent law, and by what his understanding has reached of the beginnings of origination from its ways, and by taking his action as the principle of rulings at every moment, without regard to what was established in past time. This is the infallibility specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), the comprehensive one. So his action has no ruling except what his report of the state of its occurrence makes understood, and rulings follow his action; his action does not follow a ruling. This is the aspect of his specific infallibility, from which departure is impossible. Therefore whoever among the great Companions came to this meaning would not hesitate in any of his matters, such as al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and as 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, was in following him, even in the turning of his mount, his dyeing with yellow, his wearing of the Sabtiyya sandals, and similar things of his affairs, and the affairs of those who followed this course. Whoever imagines a ruling upon him according to the requirement of his knowledge and understanding of the matter of his law will hardly be safe from falling into a matter that refutes his claim, as Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, judged when he was praying, by continuing the act of prayer when he (ﷺ) called him, until he (ﷺ) made clear to him the deficiency of his understanding regarding Allah in His right, namely by saying: 'Did you not hear Allah say: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger﴾?' (p. 255) And like the man who said: 'Come down and cut off our noses,' and he said: 'Indeed, for you there is a day,' and he said to him in the third or fourth time: 'Come down and cut off our noses, woe to you or woe be upon you!' So when it becomes clear that his action is the principle of the ruling and the locus of information, it necessarily follows that emulating him is valid in all his states, either on the basis of clarity about the determination of the rank of the ruling, whether obligation, recommendation, or permissibility, or on the basis of absolute emulation with ambiguity about the rank of the ruling and reliance on what he (ﷺ) has of knowledge. Thus the intention of emulating him with ambiguity regarding the ruling may be more complete than acting on what its ruling has been made clear. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, put on the ihram while he was in Yemen, heading toward Makka, with the ihram of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Nothing of his (ﷺ) affairs is compromised by what occurred, namely that he issued a legal opinion on one matter and then agreed with it in another, because the one who takes this from a deficiency of knowledge of his station, from the knowledge of the mercy of Allah, His word and revelation, reduces it to conformity with the matter of the sunna of Allah and His wisdom. Like the one he gave the legal opinion that jihad expiates every sin, based on his knowledge of the mercy of Allah and the execution of His word. Then he mentioned to him what Gabriel, peace be upon him, said about excepting debt from what was sent down, according to the ruling of Allah's command in His firm law and sunna. He means, and Allah knows best, that whoever's jihad is valid, all his sins are expiated, and that the settling of debt depends on pleasing his adversary. So the report of expiation looks to the final outcome, and the report of its negation looks to the beginning. Likewise, he issued a legal opinion on abandoning pollination, based on the execution of Allah's word, and he returned them to the custom of their worldly affairs when they did not bear the patience until the manifestation of Allah's word, according to their established custom. Thus many who did not doubt the implementation and validity of his ruling acted on his first legal opinion and lost the fruits of three years, then returned, without need of pollination, to a better state than their former custom. Whoever's affair is, in every event, directed by him will not fall short in attaining this, except one to whom support has not been granted to know a share of his station. When this becomes clear, then every action the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed: if it was a clarification of an obligation, it saves from the punishment of Allah; and if it was a teaching of nearness to Allah, it is a means to the love of Allah, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31]. And if neither of the two is clear to him in general, he follows it with ambiguity, which his action suffices for, and his intention elevates it. What was specific to him requires that the matter of its specificity be made apparent by a address from Allah, the Glorified, or from him, peace be upon him, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿exclusively for you, apart from the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50]." End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 25:

Since the one who is asked to respond may say, "I am only obliged to answer for myself, and I am not obliged to expose myself to harm by taking hold of the hand of another," He, glorified is He, pointed out that this is a rejection of the religion and an uprooting of it from its foundation. This is because leaving the disobedient to his disobedience is like leaving the disbeliever to his disbelief, and that necessitates the generality of affliction and an increase in decree. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And beware of a trial﴾, meaning, an affliction that overwhelms and destroys, which will encompass you if you do not guard against it. This was originally the structure, but since the prohibition against the trial reaching them was more forceful than framing it as a conditional, and more forceful than forbidding them from exposing themselves to it, because it conveys the image of its presence and their understanding of the prohibition, He used that phrasing. And since the prohibition against the trial singling out the wrongdoer was more forceful in conveying the message, He commanded them to make it general. Responding to the command, He said: ﴿Surely it will not strike﴾, and the emphatic nūn was attached because it carries the meaning of a prohibition. ﴿Those who have done wrong﴾, meaning, those who, by agreeing to disobedience, did what only one without light would do, ﴿among you﴾, O you who are commanded to be mindful of God, ﴿in particular﴾, meaning, rather it will encompass all of you. So this is a prohibition against the trial, and what is intended is a prohibition against engaging in it: that is, let none of you commit the sin, lest its effect strike you all in general; or let none of you engage in the causes of punishment while the others approve of it, lest God encompass you all with it. This is like: "I will not see you here," meaning: "Stay here, and I will see you." So the estimated sense is: place between yourselves and the general affliction a protection by setting right your mutual relations, uniting your word upon the command of God, and returning whoever opposes to the command of God, and do not dispute as you disputed concerning the matter of the spoils, lest you falter and a general punishment from your enemies or others be imposed upon you. If the obedient among you is stronger than the disobedient, or not weaker than him, and yet does not restrain him, then all have shared in the wrongdoing: this one by his act, and that one by his consent. Thus the punishment becomes a punishment of retribution for all. Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and al-Nasa'i, whom al-Tirmidhi graded as good (ḥasan), related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, that he said in a sermon he delivered: "O people! You recite this verse and interpret it contrary to its interpretation: ﴿O you who believe, take care of yourselves; those who go astray cannot harm you if you are guided﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 105]. I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'No people among whom sins are committed, while among them is one who is able to forbid them but does not do so, will fail to have God soon encompass them with a punishment from Him.'" And in al-Tirmidhi, graded as good, from Hudhayfah, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, you must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, or God will soon send upon you a punishment from Himself, then you will call upon Him and He will not answer you." And in Imam Ahmad, from him, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "You must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and urge one another toward goodness, or God will utterly destroy you all with a punishment, or He will set over you your worst, then your best will supplicate and not be answered." This is in the ruling of the attributed-to-the-Prophet (marfū') because it is not said from personal opinion. If the obedient is weaker than the disobedient, then it is to be understood in light of what Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, graded as good by him, and Ibn Majah related from Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, may God be pleased with him, that it was said to him: "How do you interpret this verse: ﴿Take care of yourselves﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 105]?" He said: "By God, I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'Rather, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, until you see stinginess obeyed, desire followed, the world preferred, and every person of opinion pleased with his own opinion; then take care of yourself and leave aside the matter of the common people, for behind you are days of patience, in which holding on to patience is like grasping a hot coal. For the one who acts in them is given the reward of fifty men who act as he does.'" He said: "O Messenger of God! The reward of fifty men from among them?" He said: "The reward of fifty from among you." Hadiths on the like of this are numerous, (p-259) and in that case the punishment becomes a vengeance upon the disobedient and a mercy for the obedient, and they will be raised upon their intentions.

When He, glorified is He, warned them of the generality of affliction, He followed it with informing them that He is powerful and is the Lord, so that they would keep to the path of uprightness. So He said: ﴿And know that God﴾, that is, the One to whom belongs the encompassing of the attributes of greatness, ﴿is severe in punishment﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 26:

Since among the severest punishments is humiliation, He warned them of it by reminding them of the abasement they had been in, for that is more effective in producing gratitude and more restraining from disbelief. So He said: ﴿And remember﴾, and He mentioned the object, saying: ﴿when you﴾, i.e., in the early days of Islam, ﴿were few﴾, i.e., in number.

Since the mere existence of weakness indicates the utmost weakness, He used the passive form in His saying: ﴿oppressed﴾, i.e., having no outlet for you, ﴿in the land﴾. He used the general term "the land," and what is meant is Makkah, because of its greatness, as if it were the whole earth, and because their condition in the rest of the lands was like their condition in it, or close to that. For this reason He expressed it with "the people" in His saying: ﴿you feared﴾, i.e., in a state of your gathering, so how much more so when you are scattered; ﴿that the people would snatch you away﴾, i.e., gradually, ﴿the people﴾, as birds of prey snatch their game. So He, glorified is He, warned them, by alerting them that He is able to return them to what they had been in of these conditions, through opposition among their word and leaving off the means of their unity, namely enjoining good and forbidding evil. In this there is also (p-260) an indication that when they were in that state of utmost weakness, and their word was united upon the command of God, which is His Oneness and obedience to His Messenger, He granted them shelter in a secure abode, having supported them with victory and given them good provision. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, causally connected to what precedes it: ﴿So He sheltered you﴾, i.e., in the abode of the Hijrah, as a mercy to you; ﴿and supported you with His victory﴾, i.e., through its people together with the angels; ﴿and provided you with good things﴾, i.e., the complete and pure spoils, made lawful and free of dispute, which had not been made lawful for anyone before you, and other things; ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾, i.e., so that your condition may be that of one whose gratitude is hoped for, and so you would be far from disputing over the spoils. This is an indication that however long they remained in that state, by turning toward the like of what had come to them and what He had increased of His bounty, He would make them masters in both abodes, through what He bestows upon them of the Criterion coming in the following verse and the success that accompanies its arrival. So the verse is directed primarily at the Companions, and it is suitable for all the Arabs, so it applies to them secondarily. Qatadah said: This tribe of the Arabs was the most humiliated of people, the most wretched in life, the hungriest in belly, the most naked in skin, and the most manifest in misguidance. Whoever of them lived, lived wretched, and whoever of them died plunged into the Fire, held down at the edge of the two mighty empires: Persia and Byzantium, eaten while not eating, and there was nothing in their lands for which they were envied, until God brought Islam, and He established them in the lands, widened their provision and spoils, and made them kings over the necks of the people. Through Islam God gave you what you see, so be grateful to God for (p-261) His blessings, for your Lord loves to be thanked, and the thankful one is in increase from God, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 27:

When He concluded the verse with what is in the utmost counsel from Him, exalted is He, to them, of sheltering, victory and good provision, which points to the favour of the Bestower's grace, and concluded that with an exhortation to gratitude, He forbade them from squandering gratitude for that by betraying His commands, through embezzlement (ghulul) or otherwise. So He said: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, as a reminder of the fidelity they had bound themselves to, ﴿do not betray Allah﴾, meaning: do not diminish the rights of the Supreme King. For the root of khawn (betrayal) is diminution, and then it was employed for the opposite of trustworthiness and fidelity, so it became a specific kind of diminution. ﴿And the Messenger﴾ by embezzlement or otherwise, but rather discharge the trust in all of that. Perhaps he repeated the governing verb in His saying: ﴿or betray your trusts﴾, of the obligations, the prescribed limits, the voluntary acts and others, as an indication that the two betrayals differ: their betrayal of Allah is literal, and their betrayal of the trust is metaphorical, because when its bearer neglects it, it is as if he has betrayed it. And He lightened it for them by His saying: ﴿while you know﴾, a state of heedlessness and the like. It is also permissible that the object is not intended, so the meaning becomes: while you are knowledgeable, and this would be an intensification of the prohibition against it, in that they are worthy that no excuse of ignorance or forgetfulness be accepted from them, because they are people of knowledge. The knower is the one who recognises Allah, and the one who recognises Him should not be separated from vigilant awareness (muraqabah).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 28:

Since the cause of betrayal is generally the love of wealth or of children, and since the cause of the disputes that led to the revelation of this surah, as explained at its beginning, was the wealth from al-Anfal (the spoils of war) [p-262], and since among the gravest forms of betrayal concerning the spoils is ghulul (misappropriating booty), and since what drives a person to ghulul is the trial of loving the accumulation of wealth, either for the pleasure of possessing it or for spending it on someone beloved, and since the child is the most cherished beloved, it was most fitting that this be followed by His saying: ﴿And know﴾, a phrase by which the listener is alerted that what follows is of the utmost importance: ﴿that your wealth﴾, whether little or great, lowly or precious, ﴿and your children﴾, likewise, ﴿are a trial﴾, meaning they are a cause of testing. God acts toward them as one who tests, so that it becomes clear to the servants who among them is deceived by the hasty and transient, and who among them has a soul elevated above that. Let this not lead you to oppose God's command, so that you perish. ﴿And that God﴾, meaning the One encompassing every perfection, ﴿has with Him a great reward﴾, both in this world and in the next, for whoever stops at His limits: He preserves his wealth for him, makes his children flourish, blesses him in them, and stores up for him in the abode of happiness. With Him is also a painful punishment for whoever neglects these. So turn with all your resolve toward Him, that you may be happy. The placement of this verse here is further enhanced by the occasion of revelation of the preceding verse, the story of Abu Lubaba, may Allah be pleased with him, whose wealth and child drove him to that act. His story concerned Banu Qurayza in the fifth year (AH), while the Battle of Badr took place in the second year.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 29:

When He reminded them of their state of weakness before the Hijrah (migration), and bestowed His favour upon them by what He had strengthened them with, and concluded this [passage] with a warning against wealth and children, which lead to ruin, and with the magnifying of what is with Him, which prompts hope, He followed this with the command to piety (taqwa), which restrains from desire, by pointing to the fear of His punishments, indicating that the combination of the two is obligatory (p. 263). He, exalted is He, explained that from it results security from others in this world and deliverance from His punishment in the next. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, repeating this description as a reminder of what its claim requires: ﴿If you fear Allah﴾, by reforming the state of affairs among yourselves, and that encompasses the whole of the religion. ﴿He will grant you a criterion (furqan)﴾, meaning victory, because the root فَرَقَ (faraqa) returns to separation. Thus, when a thing is joined, each part of it is compelled to remain attached to its companion; but when it is given the power of distinction, it is able to join and to separate. Its real meaning is: He will grant you might by which you will be able to separate from whomever you wish whenever you wish, and to join with whomever you wish whenever you wish, owing to the might of resistance that you possess, and to separate between whomever you wish whenever you wish, owing to the strength of repulsion that you have. That is, He will grant you that by which you will attain the power to act as you desire in separating and joining, which is the function of chiefs, and which returns to their saying at the time of dispute. [This is] not as you were in Makkah, when you did not feel secure in your place of residence, and could not speak, let alone argue, except with great trepidation. Even then your words had no effect by which one could be called a discriminator (fariq). The furqan among people is the one who distinguishes between matters and separates them. It is for this reason that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) was named al-Faruq, because he openly manifested Islam in Makkah in a manner that carried might and strength, making faith separate from disbelief in his presence, without fearing it. And فَرِقَ (fariqa), with a kasrah, in the sense of "he feared," also returns to what the root revolves around, for what is meant by it is: his worries were scattered (تَفَرَّقَتْ) due to the expanse of fear. And the faraq, which is the large measure, is as if it is the one that separates the rich from the poor. Al-Harawi said: it is twelve mudds (a unit of dry measure). And أَفْرَقَ مِن عِلَّتِهِ (afraqa min ʿillatihi) means he recovered from his illness, that is, a state arose that distinguished between his health and the sickness he had been suffering from. From it comes الفَرِيقَة (al-fariqah), which is a dish of dates and fenugreek cooked for women after childbirth. And قَرَفْتُ الشَّيْءَ (qaraftu al-shay') with the qaf placed first means I peeled it. And القَرْفُ (al-qarf) means mixing, as if it derives from removal, because they said that فَعَلَ (faʿala) enters into every category of meaning. From it: قَرَفَ الشَّيْءَ وَاقْتَرَفَهُ (qarafa al-shay' wa-iqtarafahu) means he acquired it, and الِاقْتِرَافُ (al-iqtiraf) in the sense of intercourse. It is possible that it returns to the vessel, because القَرَفُ (al-qaraf) is a container, since it separates what it contains from other things. And فُلَانٌ قِرْفَتِي (fulan qirfati) means the person of my suspicion, as if he had become a container for that. And فَرَسٌ مُقْرِفٌ (faras muqrif) means a horse of evident lineage, that is, a hybrid (hajin), because it is clearly distinguishable from the Arab horse. And قُرِفَ بِسُوءٍ (qurifa bi-suʾin) means he was accused of evil, that is, he was made a container for it, or his worries were scattered. And القَفْرُ (al-qafr), with the qaf placed first, means an empty place, because it is detached from people. أَقْفَرَ الْمَكَانُ (aqfara al-makan) means it became empty; أَقْفَرَ الرَّجُلُ مِن أَهْلِهِ (aqfara al-rajul min ahlihi) means he separated himself from them; قَفَرَ الطَّعَامُ (qafara al-taʿam) means the food was without condiment; رَجُلٌ قَفْرُ الرَّأْسِ (rajulun qafru al-ra's) means a man with no hair on his head, because it is detached from it; قَفْرُ الجَسَدِ (qafru al-jasad) means a body with no flesh on it; and الْقِفَارُ (al-qifar) means food without condiment. اقْتَفَرْتُ الْأَثَرَ (iqtafartu al-athar) means I followed the trace in order to separate it from others. And الْفِقْرَةُ (al-fiqrah), with the fa' placed first, and الْفَقَارُ (al-faqar) mean the vertebrae of the spine, arranged in order from the shoulder blade down to the coccyx, so that each one is distinguished from its neighbour. And فَقَرْتُ الْأَرْضَ فَقْرًا (faqartu al-ard faqran) means I dug the earth by digging, so that each part became separated from the other. And الْفَاقِرَةُ (al-faqirah) is the calamity that breaks the spine, and from it come الْفَقْرُ (al-faqr) and الِافْتِقَارُ (al-iftiqar), meaning need. أَفْقَرَنِي دَابَّتَهُ (afqarani dabbatahu) means he lent me the back of his animal. And رَامَيْتُهُ مِن أَدْنَى فِقْرَةٍ (ramaytuhu min adna fiqrah) means I shot at him from the nearest landmark, because landmarks are separated from one another. And التَّقَفُّرُ (al-taqaffur) in the leg of an animal is a whiteness, because it is separated from the rest of its colour. And رَفِقْتُ بِالْأَمْرِ (rafiqtu bi-al-amr) means I dealt gently with the matter, and that is only achieved by separating it from what harms it. From this comes الرَّفِيقُ (al-rafiq), the companion, from الرُّفْقَةُ (al-ruqfah), the group travelling together, and الْمِرْفَقُ (al-mirfaq), the elbow, from this, because of the gentleness that results from it.

Since the human being is a locus of deficiency and cannot avoid slips or lapses, He indicated this by His words: ﴿And He will expiate from you your misdeeds﴾, that is, He will cover them so long as you remain upon piety, ﴿and forgive you﴾, that is, He will erase whatever was from you that was not righteous, both in its essence and its effect. In this there is an admonition to them that the chiefs are in great peril, because they are commanded to equality among people, and the soul is naturally inclined to favour those who agree with it over those who oppose it. It is also an indication that judging with justice at the highest levels is not attained except by the rare individual. His words: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One encompassing all attributes of perfection, ﴿is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ encourage an increase beyond expiation and forgiveness from His bounty, and inform that nothing is impossible for Him. So it is possible for Him to bind each of them to the path of justice, even if that is a breach of custom at the highest level. There is also in this verse the greatest relevance to the story of Abu Lubabah (may Allah be pleased with him), because the motive that led him to punish himself was piety, so his sin was expiated and he was forgiven (p. 266). The verse was followed by this [story] as an encouragement to others to hasten to repentance when they fall into a lapse. He concluded this verse with bounty despite any deficiency, indicating His favour, exalted is He, in what He provided for the people of Islam: elevated status, the spread of awe, and the grandeur of the matter in the hearts of opponents, as is witnessed. He concluded the verse warning against compromise (mudahanah) with severe punishment, indicating the states described in the following verses, of their small numbers, their weakness, and their fear that the opponents would snatch them away. However, He, exalted is He, showed them mercy by making this [trial] come from some of them, from among those who share the name of Islam, against others, and not from outsiders. So He mixed them into factions (shiya') and made some of them taste the violence of others, so that each is afraid of the other. The pious person, because of the multitude of opponents, remains ever fearful and watchful amid perils and destructions, distancing himself and not drawing near. Yet they never lack helpers, whom Allah strengthens through them. The people of injustice continue to differ among themselves, so both sides return to them and rely upon them, and whoever they support is the one who is victorious. Thus their speech at times of constriction is the furqan. They have awe in the hearts of the wrongdoers, even if their situation becomes worse, more than the awe that the oppressors have in their hearts, so that everyone is certain that they are upon the truth, which Allah supports, and that the people of evil are upon falsehood, which Allah forsakes. Al-Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) said concerning those who are exalted on earth: "By Allah! Indeed, disobedience has humiliation in their hearts, even if flesh has grown upon them (taftafa). The fear has been divided between them in two halves, and how vast is the difference between the two parties! The fear of the people of truth, Allah increases them in reward by it and makes it a store for them, while the fear of the people of falsehood increases them in burden by it and makes it a support (azr) for His religion." This is the reality of the state in describing the people of truth and the people of falsehood.

When Allah, glory be to Him, had promised them this great favour and this momentous news, He reminded them of the circumstances of their caller, leader and guide, upon him be prayers, peace, salutation and honour, with what calls them to adhere to the means of his support, within the context of addressing him ﷺ, as a reminder of His blessing upon him and an indication of the continuation of His help to him. So He, exalted is He, said, conjoining it to ﴿when you were﴾ [al-Anfal: 26] and ﴿when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾: that is, they devised harm against you in a concealed manner. ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾: that is, they brought this description into being, and among them were some who had not yet firmly established themselves in it. Then He explained the ultimate aim of their scheming, saying: ﴿to confine you﴾: that is, to restrain you from acting freely by imprisoning you in a house whose door they would seal against you, as is clear from the story of their consultation in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh) concerning his affair ﷺ in the biographies. And whoever reads it with the letter ba' (b) followed by ya' (y), from al-bayat (the night raid), whose meaning is destroying the enemy by night, then ﴿or kill you﴾ is conjoined to it with the meaning of killing openly by day; and it is as though he regarded the night raid, as a means of catching him unawares, as nothing compared with open confrontation. ﴿Or drive you out﴾: that is, from Makkah. ﴿And they plot﴾: that is, while they plot by concealing what they intend for you of that and other forms of deceit. ﴿And Allah plots﴾: that is, He who encompasses everything in power and knowledge acts regarding their affair in the manner of one who plots by concealing what He will confront them with. ﴿And Allah is the best of planners﴾, because no one can know what He intends to conceal, for He is the Supreme King, encompassing majesty and beauty; what takes effect is only His plotting, and what prevails is only His victory. It is as though He, exalted is He, says: Look at the fulfilment of what I promised you in the circumstances of My Prophet ﷺ, for he was alone while all the people opposed him, yet he remained steadfast in conveying the message to them and delivering counsel to them, despite the harm that reached him from them, and their harm to him only increased him in striving to convey to them what benefits them.

When he mentioned their scheming against the Messenger, he mentioned their scheming against what he was sent with. So he said, linking to ﴿when you﴾ [al-Anfal: 26], ﴿and when there are recited﴾, meaning: by any reciter who is obligated, ﴿to them Our verses﴾, meaning those which are the Criterion (al-Furqan) in majesty and greatness. They did not claim that these had an effect in that situation. Rather, ﴿they say﴾, showing their obstinacy towards them and their partisanship for what they were not given, and their claim to what they could not attain: ﴿We have indeed heard﴾. Since hearing them did not produce submission in them, the listener longed to know the cause of their turning away, so he said, giving a reason or as a new statement: ﴿If We willed﴾, meaning: at whatever time We wished, ﴿We would surely say the like of this﴾, meaning: because it is not the word of God as Muhammad claims. ﴿This is not﴾, meaning: what is recited to you ﴿except the fables﴾ (asatir), the plural of sutur, and asfar is the plural of sitr, ﴿of the ancients﴾, meaning: of the children of Adam, who wrote down in them their knowledge and their reports. Therefore it is of the kind of our speech, and its speaker is of our kind. This is the utmost arrogance, because he had challenged them to produce a piece like it, if it has, as they claim, a like. He also intensified their rebuke: what prevented them from producing something of what they claim, when between them and it, by their own assertion, there is nothing except that they wish to? (p-269) Along with their resorting to the most severe matters, the sword that destroys, in their eagerness to subdue him (ﷺ), and in view of their extreme aversion to shame and their distance from what would decide against them by defeat or by being described as liars, except that they know this would expose them and disgrace them and make them ugly for all time. The meaning is: I make this noble Prophet firm in his patience over that and in his perseverance in discharging the trust, through striving in giving counsel, in spite of what he encounters, if I deliver him from them and protect him from all the schemes they plotted against him. I did not cease to support him by following those in whom I know goodness, until I prepared for him a home and concealed for him helpers, and made his home secure with companions, and built for it pillars with the swords of friends, firm and lofty. I transferred him to that while the people of obstinacy, who are all the people of the earth, strove to prevent it, but their scheming had no effect and did not benefit them, despite the hands of their hands. I made his very transfer to it a Criterion by which he distinguishes between truth and falsehood. He came to what you see: acceptance of the matter, majesty of rank, the execution of judgment among affairs, and his religion became manifest in the fullest manifestation. So they cling to piety as he clung to it, and they persist in obedience as he persisted in it. I bestow upon you from his lordship, and I clothe you with the garments of his leadership.

(p-270) When this was a matter of wonder, given that God did not hasten punishment for those who went astray and gave them respite until He struck them at the Battle of Badr, especially in light of His saying ﴿If you seek a decision, then the decision has certainly come to you﴾ [al-Anfal: 19], He explained the secret behind this, even though they pressed for its hastening. He said: ﴿And when they said﴾, meaning, out of a desire for obstinacy and to give the people the impression that they were certain it was false, since otherwise they would not have made this supplication: ﴿O Allah﴾, meaning, O You to whom belongs complete sovereignty and all-encompassing dominion, ﴿if this is﴾, meaning, the matter that Muhammad has brought to us, ﴿the truth﴾, meaning, not what we are upon, ﴿from You﴾, sent down from Your presence. Al-Zajjaj said: "No one, to my knowledge, has read 'al-haqq' in the nominative case." Abu Hayyan transmitted this.

﴿Then rain down upon us stones﴾. Perhaps the restriction of this with His saying ﴿from the sky﴾, although rain can only come from the sky, is to remove the misconception of one who imagines that "raining down" is a metaphor for stoning in general, and that it was mentioned only to show that the stones they were pelted with were as numerous as rain. ﴿Or bring us a painful punishment﴾, meaning, other than stones. Perhaps their intention in saying this was to indicate that the descent of revelation to you from the sky is an extraordinary thing, just as the arrival of stones from it is likewise extraordinary. So, if you are truthful about revelation coming to you from the sky, then bring us stones from it, just as stones came from it upon the People of the Elephant (Ashab al-Fil), as a protection from God for His House, which the army intended to violate, and as an exaltation of it. Abu Hayyan pointed this out.

This verse and the one before it were revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, whom al-Miqdad captured on the day of Badr. The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that he be killed. Al-Miqdad said: "My captive, O Messenger of Allah!" He said: "He used to say what he said about the Book of Allah, the Exalted." Al-Miqdad, may Allah be pleased with him, returned to his statement, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, enrich al-Miqdad from Your bounty." Al-Miqdad said: "That is what I wanted, O Messenger of Allah!" So the Prophet (ﷺ) killed him. His sister Qutaylah then recited verses of poetry, among them:

*"What would it have cost you had you shown grace? Often a young man shows grace even while enraged and wrathful."*

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Had this poetry reached me before he was killed, I would have shown him grace."

And from Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said to a man from Saba': "How ignorant your people were when they made a woman their king!" The man replied: "My people are more ignorant than your people." They said: ﴿If this is the truth from You﴾, and they did not say: "Then guide us to it."

The secret which He explained in this verse regarding their being given respite is that what prevented Him from hastening to answer their supplication, as He did at the Battle of Badr, was nothing but the exaltation of the station of His Messenger (ﷺ) among them. So He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 33:

﴿And Allah would not﴾ meaning: together with what He has of the attributes of perfection, greatness and majesty. He emphasized the negation with His words: ﴿punish them﴾, meaning: to renew this for them at some time or other, ﴿while you are﴾ meaning: O most noble of creation, ﴿among them﴾, for indeed one eye is repaid with a thousand eyes and is honoured...

When he (al-Biqa'i) explained the blessing of his (the Prophet's) presence, he followed it with what replaces him ﷺ when he is absent from among the servants of punishment, and so He said: ﴿And Allah would not﴾, meaning: He who possesses all perfection, ﴿punish them﴾, meaning: establishing the attribute of punishing them in a manner that endures, ﴿while they seek forgiveness﴾, meaning: they ask for forgiveness through supplication, or they utter this phrase, saying: "I seek forgiveness from Allah." Although its wording is a statement, it is in fact a supplication and a request. Thus his ﷺ presence among a people is more eloquent than the negation of punishment from them. This statement is an exhortation for them to seek forgiveness and a teaching of what averts punishment from them, just as you say: "I would not strike you while you obey me," meaning: "So obey me." Imam Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas (a grammarian and Qur'an commentator) drew attention to this. In this there is a great incitement for those among the Muslims, both sincere and hypocritical, who lived in his ﷺ midst, to desire to remain in his company and to fear separation from him, and an informing of them of what they gain from the presence of his radiant self in their midst, of the magnificent blessing, as an encouragement to love him for the length of his life and to hold fast to his support in his prohibitions and commands. For the intended meaning of seeking forgiveness, Allah knows best, is requesting forgiveness with its condition of faith and obedience. It is narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him) that there were two securities for this Ummah: as for the Prophet ﷺ, he has passed away, and as for seeking forgiveness, it remains among you until the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 34:

Since this does not explicitly establish that they deserve punishment, Allah the Exalted says, connecting it to what is implied by its meaning: "And Allah would surely punish them, [if] you had emigrated away from them and they had not believed and sought forgiveness." ﴿And what is [the matter] with them?﴾ Abu Hayyan said: "The apparent reading is that *ma* is interrogative (*istifhamiyyah*), meaning: 'What [reason] do they have for being spared punishment?' This interrogation carries the sense of affirmation (*taqrir*), meaning: 'How could they not be punished, when they possess this attribute that necessitates punishment, namely their barring of the believers from the Sacred Mosque, while they are not its guardians?'" End of quote.

The sense of the statement is: "And what share do they have in ﴿that Allah should not punish them﴾, the One who possesses perfect might and majesty over the wrongdoer, and honour and gentleness toward the obedient, in this world, ﴿while they are [such that]﴾, that is, while the reality is that they deserve punishment, so it will certainly befall them, even if its time is delayed and its appointed moment is postponed, [and it will befall them] in a manner that will make them forget the pleasures they have enjoyed, however great their worth in their eyes and however long their enjoyment has lasted; ﴿because they bar﴾, that is, they bring about the barring ﴿from the Masjid﴾, that is, from whoever wishes to venerate it through the prayer for which the mosque was built and through other acts, ﴿al-Haram﴾, that is, whose sanctity is great in the eyes of everyone, so no one has exclusive claim to it over another. That is, their conduct is the actual act of barring, in the past, present and future; they do not cease from it. Just as they used to prevent whomever they wished from entering the House and would say, 'We are its guardians; we do whatever we wish,' and they barred the believers from circumambulating it through torture and persecution. They also barred the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him by expulsion, then they barred them in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah from reaching the House, and in the year of the Umrat al-Qada from remaining beyond the three days. ﴿And [it is] not [that]﴾, that is, while the reality is that they did not have that right, because they ﴿were not its guardians﴾, that is, they were not worthy of its guardianship such that their barring would fall in its proper place.

Al-Bukhari narrated in his *Tafsir*: "On the authority of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: Abu Jahl said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. So the verse was revealed: ﴿And Allah would not punish them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33] up to ﴿from the Sacred Mosque﴾."

When He had negated their guardianship, He mentioned its people, saying:

﴿Its guardians are only﴾, that is, by right, ﴿the God-fearing﴾, that is, those who excel in this attribute by placing between themselves and the wrath of Allah the protections of obedience. [This applies] not to everyone who believes, but specifically to the believers, and they are not such [now] because they are presently tainted with disbelief. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, that is, they have no knowledge of matters by which they could distinguish between truth and falsehood, the God-fearing and the wicked, and good and bad outcomes. Perhaps He expressed it with "most" to inform that among them there are the obstinate, and because some of them later believed and became among those possessing knowledge.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 35:

Since they were doing at the House (the Ka'bah) what the House is far too pure to be associated with, being utter ignorance, He said, explaining their ignorance, their deserving of punishment, and their distance from deserving His guardianship: ﴿Their prayer at the House was not﴾, meaning the prayer that ought to be founded on humility (khushu'). He added to their disgrace with His words ﴿at the House﴾, meaning: their act, which they count as prayer or substitute for prayer, ﴿except whistling﴾, meaning a whistling resembling the whistling of birds, and ﴿clapping﴾ of the hands, which is the sound of wind from the rear. This is from makā yamkū makwan wa mukā'an, when one whistles with the mouth or interlaces the fingers and blows into them. Makkat al-shajarah bi-rīhihā means the tree sounded with its wind, and al-dubur bi-rīh al-hadath means the rear sounded with the wind of the breach of wudu'. Abu Hayyan said: it has come in the pattern fu'āl, i.e., with a dammah, and fu'āl is common for sounds, as in al-surākh (shouting). End of quote.

﴿Clapping﴾ means handclapping. The people of the Jahiliyyah used to circumambulate the House naked, whistling with their mouths and clapping with their hands in a shortened manner (muqsūrah). Their noise resembled the echo that returns sound in an empty place. So it is a metaphor that their prayer has no meaning. Its root is ṣadda (a doubled root), meaning he turned away and inclined, like al-taẓannī from ẓannana. Thus this is play, not worship, and mockery, not seriousness, although the matter is serious, and what seriousness it is, as God Most High said: ﴿Do you then wonder at this statement?﴾ [al-Najm: 59] ﴿And you laugh and do not weep?﴾ [al-Najm: 60] ﴿And you are proud?﴾ [al-Najm: 61], meaning: you do not weep in your state of seriousness with your constancy in righteous deeds. So what they do is contrary to the condition of the House; it is destruction, not construction.

Muqatil said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in the mosque, two men of the polytheists would stand on his right whistling and clapping, and two likewise on his left, to confuse his prayer."

The construction of the sentence according to the reading of al-A'mash, with ṣalātahum in the accusative, is: "There was nothing but whistling and clapping as their prayer." Thus He negated for what they consider prayer everything except whistling and clapping (mukā'an wa-taṣdiyatan), so prayer is restricted to these two in this sense. By this route it has become, in meaning, the same as the well-known recitation. So reflect on it, for it is very precious. The disagreement is derived from this in the verse of al-An'am, ﴿Then their trial would not be﴾ [al-An'am: 23], and elsewhere, and what was mentioned there benefits here.

It must be known that God did not censure these people with the highest censure. Rather, He censured them because they made worship into play, to alert through this to the censure of whoever resembles them in that, who takes what is permissible in its origin and makes it a religion. How much more so if it is disliked, or how much more so if it is forbidden. May God curse a people who claimed to have turned away from the world and then took drums, singing and clapping as their emblem, then persisted in it until they did it in the mosques, and added to the Jahiliyyah practice the dancing that the people of al-Samiri invented when they worshipped the calf. They took kinds of the actions of kinds of disbelievers and made them their habit, emblem and religion. Indeed they violated the sanctities of the Sacred Law, altered it, belittled it and held it in contempt.

Since the course of the speech is to show that they deserve punishment, and that nothing prevents it from them, and since in this battle He had already inflicted its beginnings upon them, and since the rebuke is directed at them at the time of inflicting what cannot be borne upon the enemy as a blow, He said, as a consequence of the ugliness of what they were committing: ﴿So taste the punishment﴾, meaning the punishment God promised you, which you saw at Badr and which you sought in your request for a ruling by mocking it, ﴿because you used to disbelieve﴾, meaning: by this act you have become deserving of tasting it, because of what you conceal from this clear truth that your minds pointed you to.

When He, glory be to Him, had informed about the states of the disbelievers regarding their physical actions, and their defeat despite their large numbers and strength was considered unlikely, He informed about what brings it closer, clarifying their financial actions, and said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., despite their numbers, because they veiled the mirrors of their intellects, which are the human being in reality, and thereby they fell short in a deficiency whose true nature cannot be grasped. ﴿spend their wealth﴾, i.e., they resolve to spend it in what is to come. ﴿so that they may bar﴾, i.e., by their own assumption, themselves and others, ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, i.e., from following the path whose greatness is not matched by any greatness, despite its breadth, clarity and ease. ﴿Then they will spend it﴾ [p. 277] i.e., by a compelling decree that they cannot escape. ﴿Then it will be﴾, i.e., after a period of spending it, and He expressed it with a phrase clearly showing its harm, saying: ﴿upon them﴾, and He intensified this by making the verbal noun the object of it, saying: ﴿a regret﴾, i.e., for its loss and its failure to have effect. ﴿Then they will be overcome﴾, i.e., just as happened to them at Badr, the same. For they spent despite their numbers and strength, and none of that availed them anything of what Allah intended for them; rather it became a burden upon them, for it was a cause of their boldness until they advanced, looking only at the present and failing to see the unseen, like cattle, so they perished. That was a strength for the believers, and in reality it was nothing but for them. This statement applies to what was the occasion of the revelation of the verse and to everything resembling it. That is because when they were defeated at Badr, Abu Sufyan said to them: "It is proper that you spend the wealth of that caravan," meaning the one that had been with him, "and we urge one another to fight Muhammad." They complied and spent it on the expedition of Uhud, and they achieved some success there, then regret and defeat followed them at Badr, the appointed meeting, and everything after it. Then He made manifest their attribute for which they deserved that, attaching the judgment to it and generalizing it as a warning to them of what is even more severe than that, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., it is judged that their disbelief will persist in general, whether or not they added to their disbelief the action mentioned above. ﴿To Hell﴾, i.e., not to anything else.

Since what is painful is the gathering, not its being from a particular source, He put the verb in the passive form, saying: ﴿they will be gathered﴾, i.e., after death. So they are in lasting disgrace, in this world and the next. It is permissible to use "Hell" figuratively for its causes, so the meaning would be that they are led step by step through engaging in its causes [p. 278] toward it, and are carried in this world toward it. These verses, together with their informing about what awaits them in this world and in the Hereafter, namely that the final outcome of their affair in this world is defeat, as time revealed, being one of the signs of prophethood, and in the Hereafter Hell, are also clarifying their lie in their saying: ﴿If we willed, we would say the like of this﴾ [al-Anfal: 31]. For if they were truthful in their claim, they would have said the like of it. Then they said: "If this were the truth and nothing else, we would not have said the like of it," in the place of their saying: ﴿If this is indeed the truth﴾ [al-Anfal: 32] to the end. As for the verse about whistling and clapping, it is as if it says: "This Qur'an is at the highest rank of eloquence, and you, despite your claim of precedence in eloquence, were not qualified to oppose it with anything possessing any fitness for eloquence; rather you descended to the sounds of dumb animals in reality." So nothing is clearer than this demonstration against what you claimed of falsehood and slander. As for the verse about spending, it says: "If you had been able, in opposing it, to spend words, you would not have turned away from it to spending wealth, which leads to suffering terrors, the corruption of bodies, and the perishing of the spirits they contain, leading to everlasting humiliation through eternal punishment."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 37:

When He mentioned the gathering of the disbelievers, He mentioned its cause, saying, linking it to "yuhsharun" (they will be gathered): ﴿That Allah may distinguish﴾, i.e., He Who possesses the attributes of perfection, by that gathering, ﴿the evil from the good﴾. That is: He only made for the disbelievers an abode specific to them, and they specific to it, in order to manifest justice and grace, by distinguishing the disbeliever from the believer. So He made for each abode, by which it is distinguished, justice regarding the disbelievers and grace toward the believers. Thus He places the good in a spacious, pleasant place. ﴿And place the evil﴾, i.e., the group characterized by this attribute, ﴿one upon another﴾. And "al-rakm" (piling up) is the gathering of a thing, one part upon another. So His saying, ﴿and heap it all together﴾ is an explanatory conjunction (ʿaṭf tafsīr) that emphasizes what preceded it in the intended reality, while conveying the intensity of connection, until the whole becomes like a single thing, like the piled-up cloud. The result is His saying, ﴿and cast it into Hell﴾, i.e., the abode of narrowness, distress, frowning, and worry.

Since this is a matter in which there is no success, He resumed His saying, comprehensively and explicitly with generality: ﴿Those﴾, i.e., the remote, the hateful, whom the noun of genus (ism al-jins) in "al-khabīth" made understood, ﴿they are the losers﴾, i.e., exclusively, because of the extremity of their loss, for they bought, with their wealth, the destruction of their own selves through that gathering.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 38:

When He had explained their misguidance in their bodily and financial worship, and since in many of the preceding expressions the disbelievers were cut off by the past tense with wretchedness, this could suggest that it refers to one who committed disbelief in the past, even if he repents, so that he would be despairing of repentance, and this would make him persist in disbelief. God, the Exalted, said, kindly toward His servants, guiding them to the path of rightness and clarifying the way out of the ruin they are in, in answer to one who, as if it were said: Do they have no natural disposition (jibillah) by which they might escape from loss? ﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾, meaning: for the sake of those who disbelieve, that I accept the repentance of whoever among them repents by the mere fact of his ceasing from his state, ﴿if they desist﴾, meaning: if there renews for them, at some time, the ceasing from their opposition by ceasing from their disbelief, so that they humble themselves before God and submit to His commands, ﴿they will be forgiven what has passed﴾. It is built in the passive because the beneficial thing is the forgiveness itself, which is (p. 280) the erasing of the sin, ﴿what has passed﴾, meaning: whatever they have committed, whatever it was, so it is erased both in essence and in trace, and there is no punishment for it and no reproach. ﴿And if﴾, meaning: and if they remain steadfast in their disbelief and ﴿return﴾, meaning: to opposition, ﴿then the way (sunnah) of the former ones has already passed﴾, meaning: it has come to be, has ended, and has been carried out, so there is no turning it back, by the evidence of what has been heard of the reports of those who passed away and what has been witnessed of the condition of the people of Badr, which necessitates the certainty that God is with the believers and against the disbelievers, that whoever has God with him is helped, and whoever has God against him is abandoned, seized and subdued. ﴿God has decreed: I and My messengers will surely prevail﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21]. ﴿God will surely help whoever helps Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]. ﴿And the final outcome is for the righteous﴾ [al-Qasas: 83], even though war is a matter of alternating turns.

Al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar, on Surah 8, verse 39:

When the ending of the verse indicated fighting them if they persist, and the implied meaning was: "Advance upon them wherever they confront you, advancing like bold lions, not fearing their multitude or their strength, for Allah will forsake them," he followed it with a clause stating the purpose explicitly: ﴿And fight them﴾, i.e., constantly, ﴿until there is no fitnah﴾, i.e., no cause that would necessarily incline one away from the religion at all, ﴿and religion is entirely for Allah﴾.

Since this encounter had sent the battalions of its awe into hearts, so that it struck with full force, constricting and weakening the breasts of the disbelievers while expanding and strengthening the hearts of the believers, this context called for emphasis, so He said: ﴿entirely for Allah﴾, i.e., for the Supreme King, purely, not mixed with any kind of fear or overlooking of some impurity. The root of fitnah is a mixture that alters a thing (al-fitnah: al-khaltah al-muhilah, "a mixture that changes its state"). This implies that the cause must be a great one, since a thing is not altered from its state except by a great matter, because opposing what is familiar is difficult. From this comes al-natf (plucking), and similarly nafatat al-qidr (the cooking pot overflowed), which is when the broth boils over and sticks to its sides. Al-tanufah is the desert wasteland, because it is the place of that. It also implies sincerity (al-ikhlas), from fatantu al-dhahab (I melted the gold), when you refine its good from its bad. Sometimes the inclination is toward the bad, which is the more common, and sometimes toward the good. From this comes: ﴿And We tested you with trials﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40].

Since they had two states at the time of encounter, Islam and submission on one hand, and disbelief, aversion and neglect on the other, He said, explaining the ruling for the two categories: ﴿But if they desist﴾, i.e., from fighting you by confronting you with Islam, then accept from them and cease from harming them, and do not say, "They are seeking refuge through that without sincerity," holding to the emphasis of "all of it," for it is not incumbent upon you except to turn them back from outward opposition, while the inward is with Allah. ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, i.e., who encompasses all things in knowledge and power, and He placed the prepositional phrase first for emphasis, to convey that knowledge of it is, as it were, specific to Him, so He said: ﴿of what they do﴾, i.e., however subtle it may be, ﴿is All-Seeing﴾, so He will recompense them for it. As for you, you do not know the outward and the inward together, so your duty is to accept the outward. And Allah, of what you yourselves do as well, whether restraining from them or killing, for the sake of Allah or for the sake of one's own portion, is All-Seeing, so He will recompense you according to the realities of matters and their inner aspects, even if you display to people what establishes your excuse, and He will complete for each of you the reward of what he had resolved to undertake of fighting them had they not desisted; and if they did not desist but instead advanced against you in fighting, this would have been the original form. But He, glorified is He, expressed it with His saying:

"And if they turn away" — that is, from accepting (the call), giving them the good news of their defeat and their lack of steadfastness, because of the terror that He cast into their hearts. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Know that Allah is your Mawla (protector)﴾ — that is, the One who has complete encompassing of everything — ﴿your Mawla﴾, that is, the one who manages your affairs. He acts with you as one who takes charge of the affairs of someone he loves acts: striving to obtain what benefits them and to repel what harms them. So He is, without doubt, your Helper. Then He resumed praising Himself with what He is worthy of, to make His station known and to encourage taking Him as protector, and so He said: ﴿How excellent a Mawla!﴾ He did not introduce the particle of causation (fa') here, because what is commanded is knowledge, and the belief that He is a Mawla is obligatory in itself, not for anything else. This differs from what occurs at the end of the Hajj passage, where what is commanded there is holding fast (i'tisam). ﴿And how excellent a Helper!﴾ — that is, do not fear them at all, even if their numbers increase and their might grows strong; so do not leave them until there is nothing but the Word of Allah.

(p-283) Since the sense intended is: "If your Master helps you against them, and you overcome them and gain spoils from them, then do not attribute any act to yourselves. Rather, know that He alone is the Doer, because all acts are nullified in comparison with His act. So do not dispute over the booty as one who took it by his own strength and possessed it by his own power." He then joined to this His words: ﴿And know﴾, beginning with this command to indicate that what follows is of great importance, so that they would exert effort to clear their minds to understand it, take it in properly, and observe it. ﴿That﴾, i.e., whatever, ﴿you gained as booty﴾. The ghanimah (booty) linguistically means gaining something, and in the law it is what comes into the hands of the Muslims of the wealth of the unbelievers by force, with horses and mounts. He extended the generality further, to the smallest thing possible, by His words: ﴿of anything﴾, i.e., even a thread or a needle, for all of it belongs to Him, because He alone is the Helper, and you are merely instruments, having no power to resist the enemies, since they are all the people of the earth, and you have no proportion to them in number or strength at all. So the course of justice customary among you would be that He take all of it and not allow you any of it, as was the case with those before you, when it was burned and a fire descended from heaven and consumed it. But He, glorified is He, knowing your weakness, bestowed favor upon you with it and was content from you with a fifth of it, named it for Himself, and returned it to you. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿then to God belongs a fifth of it﴾, i.e., to Him to whom all things belong, ﴿its fifth﴾.

Since it is known that God, exalted is He, is too great to be reached by benefit or harm, it is known that the mention of His name, glorified is He, is only to inform that the surrender of this fifth and relinquishing it has no share of the self in it, but is purely for religion, seeking nearness to Him, glorified is He. So He mentioned its disbursement by His words: ﴿and to the Messenger﴾, i.e., a portion of this fifth is paid to him as long as he is alive, so that he may spend it on the interests of the Muslims, and after him it is paid to his successor, who does with it what he (ﷺ) used to do. ﴿And to the near relatives﴾, i.e., of the Messenger, who are the family whom the zakat is forbidden to, namely the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib. ﴿And the orphans﴾, i.e., because of their weakness, ﴿and the needy﴾, because of their incapacity, ﴿and the wayfarer﴾, i.e., the traveler, because journeys are occasions of need. The conclusion is that He, glorified is He, did not diminish you of the booty in any way. So recognize His favor upon you: first, by bestowing victory; second, by making the booty lawful; third, by enabling you to have the four fifths; and fourth, by returning the fifth to you. Then busy yourselves with thanking Him, rather than being heedless of this, and rather than imagining that you have some act by which you deserve anything, and still less acting in disputing over the booty as one who is certain of entitlement. Know all of this with the knowledge of one who believes and affirms, submitting to what he knows, so that the fruit of action may arise from it: ﴿if you are﴾ truthful in your claim that ﴿you believe in God﴾, i.e., the One to whom no command belongs alongside Him, ﴿and in what﴾, i.e., and in Him who, ﴿We sent down﴾, i.e., a single swift sending down, for the purpose of relieving you of the Qur'an, the angels, the tranquility in your hearts, and other things previously described, ﴿upon Our servant﴾, i.e., he who always sees that all acts belong to Us, and so he attributes nothing to himself except through Us, ﴿on the day of the Criterion﴾, i.e., the Day of Badr, on which We made for you a might through which your words and deeds take effect in deciding matters.

When He, glorified is He, described it as the Criterion, reminding them of the blessing, He explained it by describing their condition, completing that (or as a substitution from it), and said: ﴿on the day the two hosts met﴾, i.e., without intention from either party, but purely by God's arrangement, ﴿the two hosts﴾, i.e., the two of which one is you, and you were, at the time of seeing each other, were you not for Our favor, certain of death; and the other is your enemies, who were certain that you were in their grip. This is the course of customary patterns. Had it been said "the day of Badr," it would not convey these benefits.

Since the reversal of the matter in victory is a place of wonder, He concluded the verse with His words: ﴿and God is over all things﴾, i.e., of granting victory to the few over the many and the reverse, and other matters, all things, ﴿Competent﴾. Its conclusion with this was thus revealing the secret, removing wonder, and making clear that what was done is in accordance with the consistent ways of His custom, the ancient practice known to those who know His past days in all the ages gone by.

When he mentioned to them the Day of the Criterion, the day of their encounter, he depicted for them their condition, which made the matter clear and showed what they were in, namely their admission of weakness. This was to remind them of that, to restrain them from dispute and to bring them back to obedience. So he said, in apposition to ﴿the Day of the Criterion﴾ [al-Anfal: 41]: ﴿when you were﴾ encamped ﴿on the near bank﴾, meaning the nearer side toward Madinah, ﴿and they were﴾, meaning the polytheists, encamped ﴿on the far bank﴾, meaning the farther side from it, the side near the sea. The regular form would convert its waw into a ya', and it has come that way, but this form is more common, just as istaṣwaba (to find something right) is more common than istaṣāba. The word al-ʿidwa, with a kasra in the reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub, and with a damma in the reading of the others, means the side and bank of a valley. Its root, in whatever order its letters appear, revolves around agitation, and it implies nearness, settling, approaching, returning and racing, as well as the place that accepts these. So it is as if it is the place that rises above a spot, and the flood becomes a place for the enemy. ﴿And the caravan﴾, meaning the trade caravan in which was the merchandise you had set out to seize, whose leader was Abu Sufyan. The phrase ﴿lower than you﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf), (p-286) meaning: you two groups, on the side of the sea, at a distance from a village, so close that you were nearly upon it and could reach out your hands to it, a distance of three miles, as al-Baghawi said. That was their aim and their wish. Had you had the strength to attack it, you would have hurried to that edge and overcome them with death. But he who was crouching on that bank, crouching like a lion, confident in what he had of strength and numbers, prevented you from reaching what you hoped for from it. This is as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Salamah ibn Salamah ibn Waqsh (may Allah be pleased with him), when he said, disparaging them after their slaughter and destruction: "We found only bald old women; when we met them they gave us their shoulders," and he (ﷺ) answered him: "Those, nephew, are the chiefs. Had you seen them you would have feared them, and had they commanded you, you would have obeyed them." This is while you considered yourselves too weak to resist them, were it not that Our messenger gave you good tidings and Our armies strengthened you. The depiction of their place and the place of the caravan points to these same meanings, indicating what the enemy had of power and strength, complete equipment, the paving of the means of victory, and the weakness of the Muslims' condition, and that their victory in such a state was nothing but a work of Allah. As for what al-Bayḍawi, following al-Kashshaf, says, that the near bank was one where feet sank and there was no water, it has already been refuted at the beginning of the surah: the well-known report in Sahih Muslim, the biographies and elsewhere is that the believers were the first to reach the water, and that the whole area of that place was sand in which feet sank; then rain fell on the Muslims, which packed the ground for them, and rain fell on the polytheists which made it impossible for them to move. ﴿And had you made an appointment together﴾, meaning you and they, to meet at those places at one time, ﴿you would have differed about the appointment﴾. That is, custom would require this for two reasons. The first is the distance you were from one another, and the difficulty of timing each group's march to match the other's. The second is your dislike of meeting them, because of what had settled in your hearts about their strength and your weakness. He who made your meeting hateful to you was able to make their meeting with you hateful to them, so the disagreement would have come from their side, as happened at the appointment of Badr. But in this battle, a summoner called them to defend others, and they could not hold back from him. Allah blinded their insight and hardened their hearts, along with the words of Abu Jahl, who was the greatest cause of the encounter, to the one who offered him support with weapons and men: "If we are fighting people, we are not weak against them; and if we are only fighting, as Muhammad claims, Allah, then no one has the strength against Allah." He also said in this battle to al-Akhnas ibn Shariq: "Muhammad is truthful and has never lied." Allah did this because He knew that your meeting them would raise His word and manifest His religion. ﴿But﴾, meaning, He arranged this, glorified is He, until you all met at the place of the encounter on one day without any appointment, and you did not differ about meeting at that place, though this went against custom, because it was the most perfect of means. He first made you covet the caravan, with your need for it, then promised you one of the two groups without specifying it, and drew Quraysh out to protect their caravan, a drawing from which they found no escape. When their caravan was saved, vainglory, show, and insolence (p-288) with their numbers and strength brought them on, as Abu Jahl said: "We will not turn back until we come to Badr, slaughter camels there, drink wine, have singing girls play for us, and feed those Arabs who are present, so that they will fear us for all time." ﴿That Allah might accomplish﴾, meaning He to whom belongs all command, by exalting His religion through your exaltation and their humiliation, ﴿a matter that was to be done﴾, as natures and dispositions are in their firmness and completeness, ﴿decreed﴾, meaning decreed from eternity: their meeting, and what befell them of slaughter and capture in that great manner. So it is certainly decreed, so that whoever believed might be clearly distinguished by his reliance on Allah and his assent to His promise, and whoever disbelieved might be distinguished too.

Since he gave this arrangement at the encounter as being for the sake of ﴿That Allah might accomplish﴾, he gave a reason for that reason in his words: ﴿that He might destroy﴾, meaning, so that seeing that supernatural decree may count, ﴿whoever was destroyed﴾, meaning of the two groups: the disbelievers during the fighting and after it, and the Muslims as well, a destruction that was transgressing and arising ﴿from﴾ a ﴿clear﴾ state, in that what became manifest of the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in this event in all that he promised, and the lying of the disbelievers in all that they were saying, asserting it firmly, though the outward situation seemed to favour them. So this was among the greatest miracles. ﴿And that whoever lived might live﴾, meaning by Islam, a life that is at the highest perfection, as indicated by the reading of Nafi' and al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim in making both yas clear; or at the least perfection, as indicated by the assimilation (idghām) of the rest for lightness, (p-289) a life that transcends and arises ﴿from﴾ a ﴿clear﴾ state, meaning one that comes after clarification, in that the disbelievers are upon falsehood and the believers upon truth, since it will come that they used to say: ﴿Their religion has deceived these﴾ [al-Anfal: 49]. Then the deceived one became evident, and the wonders of what was decreed were uncovered from the eyes of the hidden hearts.

Since the implied sense is: "Indeed Allah in doing that is Mighty and Wise," he followed it with his words: ﴿And indeed Allah is All-Hearing﴾, meaning of what you were saying and other things, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what you were concealing and other things. So humble yourselves before His greatness, and turn back from your disputing out of fear of Him.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 43:

He, glorified is He, completed the depiction of their condition with His saying, clarifying what He had alluded to of the subtlety of His arrangement: ﴿When﴾, i.e., remember when you wished to know that, when ﴿Allah showed them to you﴾, i.e., He who possesses the attributes of perfection, so He does what He wills, ﴿in your dream, few﴾, as an emphasis on what had previously been made known to you, that the encounter, let alone what resulted from it, came only from Him, and that they were like an instrument that has no choice. This is because the Prophet ﷺ saw them in his dream as few, so he informed his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, of that, and their hearts were reassured and that encouraged them. He also specified what corruption would have occurred had it not been for that, saying: ﴿And had He shown them to you﴾, i.e., in your dream or otherwise, ﴿as many﴾.

Since the reporting after the battle was of the opposite of what occurred in it, which human nature would tend to hesitate over, He emphasized His saying: ﴿you would have lost heart﴾, i.e., become cowardly, ﴿and you would have disputed﴾, i.e., differed, so each one would have taken a view contrary to the view of his companion, ﴿concerning the matter﴾, i.e., you would have become weak, and that would have increased you in weakness and aversion to meeting them. ﴿But Allah﴾, i.e., He who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, ﴿saved﴾, i.e., but He did not show them to you as such, so safety was achieved from what would have resulted from them of retreat. Then he explained the reason for His arrangement of that and His informing you of this matter that was decreed, with His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing﴾, i.e., of perfect knowledge, ﴿of what is within the breasts﴾, i.e., their inner thoughts, of boldness and cowardice and other than them, before they occur in the hearts.

When he [the Prophet (ﷺ)] had explained what resulted from seeing them as few, and what would have resulted from seeing them as many had the two groups met in that way, because he (ﷺ), out of his sincere advice and compassion for them, used to inform them of what he had seen, just as he informed them at the Battle of Uhud about the slaughtered cows, Allah followed this with the kindness He showed them in making them see the enemy with their own eyes while awake. So He said: ﴿And [remember] when﴾, meaning: and remember also when ﴿He showed them to you﴾, meaning: He let you see them ﴿when﴾, meaning: at the time when ﴿you met﴾. He drew attention to the fact that this sight was not the reality of their condition by His saying: ﴿in your eyes﴾, meaning: not in the actual reality, ﴿as few﴾, meaning: their number was small and their affair was insignificant, confirming what the Prophet (ﷺ) had told you of his vision, so that you would be emboldened against them. It was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "They were made to seem few in our eyes on the day of Badr, so much so that I said to a man beside me: 'Do you think they are seventy?' He said: 'I think they are a hundred.' Then we captured one of them and asked him: 'How many were you?' He said: 'A thousand.'"

Al-Harrali (ʿAlī al-Ḥarrālī) said in (the commentary on) Āl ʿImrān: He made "few" a description of them that is constant, fixed and permanent upon them, by what necessitated in them a deficiency of their essences, through the concealment of their natural disposition and what lies beyond the created disposition (p-291) of their essences. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and He makes you appear few﴾. The form here is a verb occurring at a particular time, not a description of them, in that if He had shown them to you in the true manner of seeing, He would have multiplied them tenfold, so that you would have seen them as three thousand and two hundred and thirty. End of quotation.

﴿in their eyes﴾, before the encounter, so that they would be emboldened to clash with you, to the point that Abu Jahl said: "They are only a people who eat camel meat." Then He made you appear many in their eyes at the moment of contact, until they fled when the multitude surprised them, and they entertained all kinds of suspicions. Al-Harrali said: He made them appear few when they did not see them in the true tenfold manner of sight, nor did they see them in the sensible form. So that was a sign for the believers, according to the reading with the third-person ya' (i.e., in Āl ʿImrān), and it was a sign for the disbelievers according to the reading ﴿you see them﴾ [al-A'raf: 27] with the second-person ta' (of address). Thus in this there was a manifestation of the sight in the eyes of both groups, similar to what occurred between the two sights between Moses (peace be upon him) and the magicians, in that Moses (peace be upon him) and those with him imagined from their magic that it was moving, and Pharaoh and those with him saw a manifest serpent swallowing what they falsely fabricated, as a true sight. Thus there is a correspondence between the preceding verses and this verse in some respect.
