This verse is more noble and subtler, in that it is a contest without any instrument of staffs or ropes, within the essences of the two groups and their perception. End of quotation.

When he had mentioned what Allah the Glorified had caused in the perception of the two groups, he gave the reason for it in His saying: ﴿so that Allah may accomplish﴾, meaning: He who possesses supreme might and manifest wisdom, of His granting you victory and their humiliation, by making your multitude surprise them after you had seen them as few, so that this would embolden them and defeat them (p-292), ﴿a matter that was to be done﴾, meaning: by means of their being taken by surprise, through the multitude that overwhelmed them after the fewness, away from caution and preparation for it, and by what He did through your hands in this battle of killing, capture and defeat, which produces the humiliation of all the people of disbelief. It was decreed from eternity, so it must come to pass as He determined, because none can repel His command and the word is not changed in His presence. He did all of that alone.

Since the sense is: the beginning of affairs is in the hand of Allah the Glorified, by His decreeing them from eternity and not by the hand of anyone other than Him, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And to Allah﴾, meaning: the Supreme King in whose hand alone is every affair, ﴿all matters are returned﴾, meaning: all of them, so that nothing is carried out except what He wills to carry out. Matters do not proceed according to what the servants suppose. This is from your saying: "This matter returns to you," meaning: whatever you intend regarding it will take effect; and even if it were supposed that someone else dealt with it, it would have no effect on it. It continues thus until it returns to you and so it proceeds. The conclusion is that there is in it the force of return in this sense, even if there is no actual return. In this there is an admonition that the affairs of this world are not sought for their own sakes, but what is intended from them is what may serve as provision for the Day of Return.

When this was established and completed upon this most judicious path and straightest method, it became the cause (ʿillah) of the content of His saying, "O you who have believed," (the two verses), so that they were its result. For whoever knows that the whole matter belongs to Him, and that there is no effect of few or many, bears fruit, for the one who is at the lowest ranks of faith, let alone others, in the lack of concern for the wrongdoers, even if their strength exceeds the limit and they increase greatly beyond count (p-293). The two verses remind them of their state which necessitated their victory, so that they would keep to it in every battle and not dispute as they disputed over the spoils. ﴿When you meet﴾, i.e., when you fight, for "meeting" (liqa') is a term predominantly for fighting. ﴿a company﴾, i.e., a group deserving of fighting, as their description as believers has sufficed in place of describing them thus. ﴿then stand firm﴾, i.e., in meeting them by fighting them, as you stood firm at Badr, and do not let your souls entertain thoughts of flight. ﴿And remember Allah much﴾, i.e., the One to whom belongs every perfection, so everything that is sought is found with Him. ﴿much﴾, i.e., as you did there, for that is a sign of sincerity in relying upon Him alone, and that necessarily brings victory, as in the hadith qudsi: "Indeed My servant, the most devoted of My servants, is the one who remembers Me at the meeting of his opponent."

When He commanded this, He gave the reason with the particle of hope, so that it would be more indicative that He, glory be to Him, is under no obligation, and so that it would be for faith. He said: ﴿so that you may prosper﴾, i.e., so that you would be in hope of success, which is attaining the desired aim of victory and reward, just as you were at that time.

﴿And obey Allah﴾, i.e., the One who possesses absolute self-sufficiency, so He accepts only what is sincere and the most perfect completion, and He does only what He wills. ﴿And His Messenger﴾, i.e., in advancing and in holding back, because you do not know the outcomes. That obedience is a sign of your sincerity in the remembrance (*dhikr*). ﴿And do not dispute﴾, by each one wanting to pull his companion's share away from him, whether in opinion or otherwise, and to establish what is his own. He pointed to the great harm of disputing by explaining its bitter fruit, saying: ﴿lest you lose heart﴾, i.e., become weak. Al-Qamus says: "*fashila*, like *faraḥa*, so he is *fashil*: he became lazy, weak, slack, and cowardly." End.

The root returns to *al-faysha[la]*, which is the glans (*al-ḥashafa*). Its necessary consequence is softness, and from softness arises cowardice together with arrogance, levity, and recklessness.

Since failure may sometimes coexist with victory, because of the enemy's failure more than your own or for some other reason, He joined what usually follows it with the conjunction *wa* rather than *fa*, saying: ﴿and your strength will depart﴾, i.e., your dominance and your power. The origin of this is that when the wind blew in battle from the direction of a line of fighters, it would be in the faces of their enemies and would prevent them from what they intended, so they were forsaken. Thus it became as if it were the strength of the one from whose side it came, and so it was used as a metaphor for that strength. Then He concluded these causes with that which gathers them together and organizes the aims of their people, saying: ﴿and be patient﴾, i.e., endure whatever hardships occur, for if you suffer, your enemies suffer likewise, while you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for. Then He gave the reason for which victory truly comes, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, i.e., the One encompassing the attributes of perfection, ﴿is with the patient﴾, i.e., because they do not endure except by relying on Him, and whoever has Him with him is mighty.

As Imam Shams al-Din Muhammad ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya said at the end of his book *al-Furusiyya al-Muhammadiyya* regarding this verse: the management of wars is the best arrangement in the most complete form. In it He commanded five things, which never came together in a band without victory, even if it was small in comparison with its enemy. The fifth is the criterion, the foundation, and the basis of all of that, which is patience. Upon these five pillars the dome of victory is built, and whenever they or some of them are removed, victory is removed to the same degree. When they come together, they strengthen one another and have a great effect. When they were gathered among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, no nation could stand against them, so they conquered the lands east and west, and people submitted to them in peace and war. When they scattered among those who came after them, and weakened, the matter gradually descended to what you see. There is no power except with Allah. What gathers all of that is obedience to Allah and His Messenger, for it necessitates the support of the obedient one with the strength of the one whom he obeys. This is the secret of the saying of Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, which al-Bukhari narrated in the chapter "A righteous deed before fighting": "You only fight people by your deeds." It is an ancient legislation. In the course of the fifth book of the Torah it says: "If you hearken to the voice of the LORD your God and observe to do all His commandments which I command you this day, the LORD your God will set you on high above all the nations of the earth. You shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow, and you shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 47:

When He, glory be to Him, had reminded them of what made their victory necessary, commanding them to remain steadfast in it, He mentioned to them the state of their enemies, which made their defeat necessary, forbidding them from it. This was an allusion to the state of disputing over the spoils (al-anfal), and that it is the state of one who desires this world. If it persists, it is close to dragging them into the state of those whose aim is this world. So He said: ﴿And do not be﴾, that is, O company of (p-296) believers, ﴿like those who﴾. He described the ugliness of their deed from beginning to end, saying: ﴿went out from their homes﴾, that is, each one from his home, and they were the people of Makkah. Anyone who does the same as their deed is like them. For this reason He expressed it by the description, so that it would be general. ﴿Insolently﴾, that is, with transgression and arrogance against the truth. The root بطر (baṭar), in whatever order its letters are arranged, revolves around softness that is receptive to work, until it is bound, for were it not for weakness, what is bound could not be secured. From it come baṭr al-jurḥ (lancing a wound, which is cutting it open) and al-bayṭār (the farrier, one who treats animals). Sometimes that softness comes from bewilderment. From it comes abṭartu ḥilmahu, meaning I bewildered him and took his forbearance away from him, and dhahaba damuhu baṭaran, meaning his blood was lost in vain, due to weakness in it, from confusion about the matter that leads to it. Sometimes it comes from exceeding the limit in hardness. From it comes baṭara al-ni'mah, meaning one who does not thank for a blessing, so he exceeds the limit in exultation. The one who does this, the Wise One enables him to reach his fatal points, and He seizes him while he is returning to the inability of his powers to bear gratitude. So the doer of this is weak, even if the opposite of that appears from him, as ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Justice, even if it appears gentle, restrains me from injustice more than oppression does, even if it appears severe," or as he (may Allah be pleased with him) said. What is closer to this is that the root revolves around mixing that transfers from one state to another.

When He mentioned what drove them to go out from themselves, He mentioned what made it necessary for them from other than themselves, saying: ﴿and to be seen by people﴾, that is, they went out wanting to show people their going out and what results from it, so that people would say about it what they say. When it was said to them, "Allah has saved your caravan, so turn back," they became insolent in their blessing, following Abu Jahl when he said: "By Allah, we will not return until we reach Badr, drink wine, slaughter camels, and have singing girls play for us, so that the Arabs will hear of us and will always fear us forever!" So they were given cups of red death instead of wine, and the mourners of time wailed over them instead of the music and singing girls.

When He mentioned the going out itself and the corruption in it, and mentioned its evil fruit arising from those two traits, He expressed them by the noun to indicate their permanence, as is the nature of character traits, and expressed the fruit by the present tense to alert that they continually renew it. So He said: ﴿and block [others]﴾, that is, they create blocking, which is prevention, for themselves and for others, ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King in that respect, while they are resolved to renew that at every time. Since these were their aims, their weaving was flimsy and their structure frail, for they are from the work of Satan, and every deed that is not for Allah collapses when it collides with what is for Allah. By this, glory be to Him, He enacted His custom, and you will not find any change in His custom, for those who work are the servants of Allah. ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, they did this while the one who encompasses everything, whom they opposed, is His friend ﴿with what﴾. Or this may be coordinated with an implied clause: so Allah, by His majesty and greatness, nullified their deeds, and He is ﴿encompassing of what they do﴾, so they are in His grip. So He brought them, when they went out opposing Him, to Badr, and He slaughtered their necks in place of the camels, gave them cups of death in place of wine, and screamed upon them with the screams of the mourners in place of the singing girls. Perhaps He placed the prepositional phrase first to indicate that, because of the intensity of His encompassing their deeds, it is as if (p-298) He has no regard for anything other than them, so nothing distracts Him from them.

Since al-Biqa'i had explained to them the corruption of their deeds, owing to the corruption of their intentions, as a warning against them, he increased the warning by directing them, through an implicit command, to keep constantly mindful of this. He used a conjunction linking to something not previously mentioned, saying: ﴿And when﴾. It is thus known with certainty that the implied sense is: "Remember that, and remember when." He further increased the warning by mentioning the clear enemy, and by alerting them that everything that commands them to evil is merely an illusion with no reality, just as what he had embellished for them in this matter was. So he said: ﴿Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾. That is, the enemy, the one who is burning (with envy) and far from good, made fair to them ﴿their deeds﴾, which they had, in their own estimation, perfected in opposing the Prophet (ﷺ). This happened because he appeared to them in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum al-Kinani, when they feared that his people, the Banu Kinanah, would harm their families in their absence, because of the enmity that existed between them, which made that fear reasonable. Thus this nearly deterred them from setting out. ﴿And he said﴾, deceiving them concerning themselves: ﴿No one among the people can overcome you today﴾. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr) is the predicate of ﴿لا﴾ (lā); otherwise its subject would have been in the accusative, because in that case it would have resembled a construct phrase (idafah). ﴿Today, among the people﴾. He also deceived them regarding those they had left behind, by his saying: ﴿And I am your protector﴾, from Kinanah doing you harm with anything you dislike. He marched with them to Badr, encouraging them, reciting verses to them, and inciting them by this outward statement, toward what he whispered to them in their hearts. ﴿Then when the two hosts came into view﴾, that is, each host saw the other, and he saw Jibril, peace be upon him, among the armies of Allah. ﴿He turned back﴾, that is, he retreated walking backwards, and his scheme and the traces of his whispering were nullified, ﴿on his heels﴾, that is, backward. They said (p-299): "Where [are you], O Suraqah?" They did not suppose him to be anyone but Suraqah. So he passed on, did not answer them, and did not turn aside to them. ﴿And he said﴾, that is, by the tongue of his state or by speech, whether they heard it or did not hear it: ﴿Indeed, I am free of you﴾. Then he gave the reason for his disavowal of them by his saying: ﴿Indeed, I see﴾, that is, with the eye of my sight, ﴿what you do not see﴾, that is, the angels and the wrath that is descending upon you. Al-Harith ibn Hisham, whose hand was in his hand, said to him: "By Allah, we see nothing but the spies of Yathrib!" Then he resumed his speech, emphasizing his rejection of their claim, by saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah﴾, that is, the One who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, lest He destroy me along with you by swift punishment. ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿is severe in punishment﴾. They then said: "Suraqah has fled from us." He replied: "It has reached me that you are saying such-and-such! By Allah, I had no knowledge of this march of yours except when news of your defeat reached me." They kept denying him until they embraced Islam, and then they knew that the one who had deceived them was Satan. This is well known in the biographies (sirah) literature. It is more appropriate to interpret this as mere whispering rather than an actual appearance. And in a hadith: "Iblis was never seen on any day more humiliated, more abased, or more enraged than on the Day of 'Arafah, because of what he sees of the descent of mercy; except what was seen on the Day of Badr."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 49:

When he (Allah) had completed what He was cutting off concerning those (the believers) with respect to what comes from their own selves and what comes from the adornment of Satan, He replaced it with what is cut off concerning them, namely the people of ignorance of Allah, of His past days, and of His signs among His friends and His enemies. So He said: ﴿When the hypocrites say﴾, that is: from among the Arabs and the Children of Israel, a saying which they renew at every time because of the desire they have in it; ﴿and those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, that is: among those who believed but whose faith did not take firm root in their hearts and who did not emigrate, or among the Jews who openly declared disbelief, when they see the disbelievers and their strength and their numbers, and the believers and their weakness and their fewness: ﴿Their religion has deceived these﴾, pointing at you, ﴿their religion﴾, that is: in their advance toward what is certain to bring about their destruction, thinking that Allah is their helper, though they were three hundred and some ten and a dozen, against nearly a thousand kings of the Arabs, so that this would enrage you. Then Allah belied them and confirmed your cause through your reliance upon Him and your patience in your religion. ﴿And whoever﴾, that is: they said that knowing that you rely upon Him and that He has made you patient in your religion, ﴿and whoever﴾, that is: they said that knowing that you rely upon Him whom you follow, and the situation being that whoever ﴿relies upon Allah﴾, that is: He who has comprehensive encompassment, so He does what He wills with you and with others, provided the condition is met, namely faith and striving in obedience, as you did; for indeed He is the Mighty, the Honourer.

Since He, glorified is He, encompasses every attribute of perfection absolutely, without restriction to reliance or anything else, the Exalted made it explicit, saying, linking it to its implied sense: Indeed Allah is capable of giving Him victory: ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, that is: He to whom belongs absolute perfection, ﴿is Mighty﴾, that is: overpowering over everyone who contends with Him, so He is worthy of granting victory; ﴿Wise﴾, that is: perfectly precise in His actions; so He is fit to seize the enemy of the one who relies upon Him from the place where no stratagem will avail him.

When he had mentioned what gladdened them concerning the state of their enemies, both those who openly opposed them and those who concealed it, in this world, and had adorned that with jewels of wisdom and wondrous words, by adhering to which happiness is attained and by neglecting which misery descends, he followed it with what would gladden them concerning the state of their enemies at death and after it. He said, addressing one for whom, even if the veil were lifted, certainty would not increase, and directing the address specifically to every listener toward strength of certainty, so as to qualify him for such an address (p. 301), relating their state at that time: ﴿And if﴾, i.e., they say this while the situation is that if you ﴿saw﴾, O highest of creation, ﴿when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., completely extract the souls of ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, meaning those among these speakers and others, those whom you slew at Badr and others after that and before it, ﴿the angels﴾, i.e., their hosts whom We appointed over them, while they ﴿are striking﴾

Since striking the face and the back is the most indicative of humiliation and disgrace, He said: ﴿their faces and their backs﴾, i.e., their highest and lowest parts of the body, so other parts are more fitting [to be struck]. ﴿And﴾ while they say to them: ﴿Taste the punishment of burning﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 181], i.e., you would have seen a terrifying sight and a dreadful matter. That would have gladdened you to the utmost extent of joy, and their speech would not have affected your anger, for they will then know who it was whose religion deceived him. And although "law" (if) converts the present tense into the past, the use of the present tense within its scope is not without benefit, and that benefit is what has been mentioned: an indication that this does not apply to one dead among them rather than another dead, but there is no difference between their earlier and later ones, whether they died at Badr or elsewhere. There is nothing in the speech requiring that those who said ﴿These people's religion has deceived them﴾ [al-Anfal: 49] must have been present at Badr. Rather, the apparent meaning is that those who said it were in Medina. Their use of "these" (ha'ulaa'), which is the particle of nearness, is for belittlement and for making their seizure seem easy, just as the particle of distance is used for magnification by distance of rank. On this same basis is interpreted the saying of Pharaoh after the Children of Israel had traveled for a time, the least of which was a night and part of a day, as God related about them: ﴿Indeed, these are a small band of few﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 54]. Moreover, al-Baghawi reported in his commentary on His saying: ﴿They see them as twice their number with their own eyes﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 13] that a group of Jews attended the battle of Badr to see on whose side the outcome would fall. If you reflect on this together with His saying: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Anfal: 52], you will know that the main intended subject of these verses, up to His saying: ﴿That is because they are a people who do not understand﴾ [al-Hashr: 13], is the Jews. In His phrasing "they do not understand" there is severe rebuke for them, as God said in the verse of al-Hashr: ﴿Indeed, you are more fearsome in their breasts than God. That is because they are a people who do not understand﴾ [al-Hashr: 13].

When they had tortured them, both by word and by deed, they gave them a reason for it, adding to their distress, saying: "That," meaning this deed, this great act that He does to you of painful punishment,

﴿because of what your hands have sent forth﴾, meaning from audacity toward God,

﴿and that﴾, meaning, and because He has the right to do that even if you had not sent forth anything, ﴿God﴾, meaning the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿is not unjust﴾, meaning not one who wrongs,

﴿to the servants﴾. His dominion over them is complete, and the one whose dominion is complete is like the king over whom nothing lies outside the circle of his rule. He is the One who created you with this evil disposition from which these ugly deeds arose, and He is not asked about what He does. Who could question Him? It is also possible that the meaning is: and He is not one who wrongs, for He does not leave the wrongdoer to transgress against the wronged without requital for your wronging the people of His obedience. [The wisdom of the expression in a form that admits of exaggeration will come later, in Fussilat.] (p-303)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 52:

Having explained, through what preceded, what requires unity and the return to Him in every matter, and having shown that whoever opposes this is destroyed, whoever he may be, he followed it with what shows that this is a general and constant law, not restricted to one time or one place. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Like the custom﴾, i.e., the habit of these disbelievers and their way, to which they persisted, continued, and kept up, becoming accustomed to it, ﴿of the people of Pharaoh﴾, i.e., those whose circumstances the Jews here know best of all people,

﴿and those who﴾. Since those destroyed for denying the messengers were some people of earlier times, he introduced the preposition and said: ﴿before them﴾. This is also among the proofs of ﴿so you did not kill them﴾ (8:17), because those He pointed to were destroyed without fighting. Rather, some were destroyed by the wind, some by the Blast, some by drowning, and some by the sinking into the earth, which is a drowning in solid ground. It is as if He is saying: let no one attribute an act to himself, for in destroying My enemies there is no difference to Me whether their destruction comes through the empowering of fighting or otherwise; all is by My act, and had it not been for Me, it would not have happened. This is a great deterrent for whoever boasts of killing someone whom God has slain at his hand, or disputes over the spoils (nafl, voluntary extra booty). This returns to His saying: ﴿so that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult in what He has given you﴾ (57:23). In this there is an urging to train oneself to be indifferent to anything in which the self has even the slightest share, so that this becomes a disposition, as was the custom of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who never ascribed any of his excellent qualities to anyone but his Creator, unless he was commanded to legislate about it. Rather, he would say: "God has slain them," "God has repelled them," "God has given us victory," "God is sufficient." When this becomes a disposition for those who hold fast to it, it leads them to praise the Creator and the created being who is praised by them, as Ka'b ibn Zuhayr (may God be pleased with him) said in praising them:

They are not exultant when their spears attain a people,
nor are they humbled when they themselves are overcome.

Then He, exalted is He, explained the condition in which they resembled those before them, by His saying: ﴿They disbelieved in the signs of God﴾, i.e., they concealed what the lights of their intellects had pointed them to of the indications of the Most High King, and covered them over, because they did not act upon them and they barred from them whoever followed them. So their recompense was what resulted from that, in His saying: ﴿So God seized them﴾, i.e., He Who possesses the totality of greatness and the bonds of majesty and might, seizing them with the seizing of overpowering, subjugation, and punishment,

﴿for their sins﴾, just as He seized them. For they dared against the rank of divinity, before whose lofty heights the eyes' glances are dazzled, before whose flashing rays the bright lights grow dim, before whose distance from the first of its ascending steps the powers are exhausted, and before whose imagined nearness the necks are cut off in its wastelands. So the thunderbolts of its awe descended upon them, and the vicissitudes of its greatness alighted upon them, so that they became such that only their dwellings could be seen and only their places of play and their abodes could be perceived.

When He had informed of their seizing, He gave the reason for it with His saying: ﴿Indeed God﴾, i.e., He to Whom belongs all-encompassing comprehension, ﴿is Strong﴾, i.e., He overcomes everything and nothing overcomes Him,

﴿Severe in punishment﴾.

[p. 304]

Then He repeated His words: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾, that is, Pharaoh and his people, for they are his followers, so it should not be imagined that they do anything without him leading them in it. ﴿And those before them﴾ — for a subtle point, which is that it has already been stated that there was no nation except that it was tested with adversity and with ease. The first (the station of Divinity, al-Ilahiyyah) looks upon the One who gazes at majesty, pride, subjugation and retribution, while the second is the fruit of the station of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah), from which arise affection, mercy, compassion and honouring. Therefore, in the first he expressed the Name of the Essence (al-Dhat), which encompasses all the attributes and whose word — according to those who hold that it is derived — is set for the meaning of Divinity, indicating that they turned away during adversity from affirmation and dealt with it through stubbornness and persistence. And for this reason, in this second one, he expressed the Name of the Lord, saying: ﴿They denied﴾, that is, (p-307) out of obstinacy, in addition to covering what reason indicates by denying what is transmitted,

﴿the signs of their Lord﴾. Thus He pointed by this to their insolence over the blessings and their denial that they were due to the supplication of the Messengers.

And when He indicated by the expression "with Him" that they were deceived by His treating them with gentleness and kindness, He said: ﴿So We destroyed them﴾, that is, all of them,

﴿for their sins, and We drowned﴾. He used the plural of majesty as an indication that He brought upon them what made them forget that kindness, ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾; and as an indication that they forgot that the Lord, just as He is characterized by mercy, must also be characterized by majesty and vengeance, otherwise His lordship would not be complete. This is clear from what preceded in al-A'raf from the Torah in explaining: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾ [al-A'raf: 133] to its end, that Pharaoh would ask Moses, peace be upon him, at every calamity to pray for its removal, pleading that the Lord is possessed of forbearance, patience and mercy. He placed the first first as an indication that they had reached the extreme of audacity, and the expression in it with "disbelieved" supports this, meaning that mere concealment of the signs by turning away from them is sufficient to necessitate retribution, even if no explicit denial was stated, because of the greatness of the station. The root k-f-r, in whatever order it occurs, revolves around mixing that inclines and confuses, and specifically in this order it revolves around concealment, that is, they covered over the affirmation of the signs of their Lord. It is also permissible — and this is the better view — that its usage, absolutely and without the restriction of order, revolves around thought (fikr), which is sending the eye of insight to seek a matter, and it entails (p-308) uncovering and concealing, for it sometimes lifts the trailing skirts of doubts from that matter so that it becomes clear and established, and sometimes it brings the decisive proofs to bear upon it so that it vanishes and is annihilated; and perhaps it lets down the trailing skirts of doubts over it so that what was clear becomes hidden, just as it had gathered them up from it so that what was hidden was revealed.

When He, glorified be He, informed of their destruction, He informed with the descriptor that comprises their destruction, saying: ﴿And all of them﴾, that is, of these and of those who preceded them from the people of Pharaoh and those before them,

﴿were﴾, that is, by disposition and nature, ﴿wrongdoers﴾, that is, to themselves and to others, placing the signs in other than their proper places while they imagined for themselves justice.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 55:

Then he gave the reason for their being described as wrongdoers, or began an explanation of it with his words: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living beings﴾, meaning: they did wrong because they disbelieved in the signs of their Lord, who alone bestowed favour upon them. And the worst of living beings ﴿in the sight of Allah﴾, meaning: in the judgment of the Just Judge, to whom belongs all command, and in His knowledge,

﴿those who disbelieve﴾, meaning: of them and of others. That is, He judged them to be bound to disbelief because of the corruption of temperament that was built into them, through their lack of suitability for goodness. Thus they had fallen from the rank of humankind to the rank of animals in general, and then to the level of insects and worms, indeed to that of the most lowly crawlers; for the worst of people are the disbelievers, the worst of disbelievers are those who persist in it, and the worst of the persistent are those who break covenants. ﴿So they﴾, meaning: because of that, ﴿do not believe﴾, meaning: no faith will be renewed among them that they would persist in, because of what preceded in Allah's knowledge concerning them. Thus they did not benefit from what came to them of the attribute of Lordship, so the attribute of Divinity destroyed them. (p-309) Perhaps he specified the family of Pharaoh as a reminder, since most of those who said ﴿These people's religion has deluded them﴾ [al-Anfal: 49] were the Jews, that in comparison with Pharaoh and his household they were weaker than the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, in comparison with the Quraysh and their followers. For the Jews, despite their small number, had submitted to them with the humiliation of slaves to their masters, indeed even more so; and despite that they were victorious over them when Allah was with them. This was also to inform them that they are now like the family of Pharaoh in obstinacy, along with what they are in of scarcity and abasement. They had gathered from every people their basest qualities and worst conditions. For this reason he made a substitution from the generality of ﴿those who disbelieve﴾:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 56:

﴿Those with whom you made a covenant﴾ — they are the Jews without doubt, whether the Banu Qaynuqa', or al-Nadir, or Qurayza, or all of them according to their distribution. Each of them broke the covenants that they had taken from him (ﷺ) and failed the promises that they had confirmed.

Since a covenant deserves fulfilment, especially from the scholars, He expressed it with His saying: ﴿then they break their covenant﴾, meaning: they renew its breaking whenever there appears to them a glimmer of a false lightning or the boasting of a hero who raids against the face of the truth. Then He magnified the outrage against them with His saying: ﴿every time﴾. Then He drew attention to their lack of fear, from the lofty rank of honour and the abyss of folly and extravagance, by not fearing the consequence of treachery, with His saying: ﴿and they do not fear﴾, meaning: neither the people in blame of them for that, nor Allah in this world by being empowered over them, nor in the Hereafter by His humiliating them and then casting them down into the Fire after the proclamation of shame.

(p-310) When He had despaired them of being godfearing, given their persistent breaking of covenants, which arises from extreme envy, stubborn necks, hard hearts, and obstinacy in disbelief, He commanded him with what weakens their strength and loosens their bonds, namely casting despair into them by sending down might. This is in keeping with the custom of Allah, glorified is He, who instructs him to show gentleness toward some people, knowing that his work thrives when built on the best foundation. So He said, emphasizing it because of the love of gentleness with which he (ﷺ) was created: ﴿So if you gain the upper hand over them in war﴾, that is, you encounter them and prevail over them,

﴿in the war﴾, that is, the war in which the falsifier is normally defeated and the truthful, who is sound, prevails,

﴿then scatter those behind them﴾, that is, inflict on them a punishment that splits and disperses from fighting you those who stand behind them, those who hold the same opinion as they do in opposing you. Do not leave them at all, for your followers are more skilled and cleverer than they are, so they are more steadfast and capable. When you inflict this on them, none will dare to oppose you after them, taking warning from them and learning from their condition. The root sh-r-d, in every arrangement, revolves around passing through and departing. If it is done with purpose and a clear path, it is guidance (rushd), and it entails gathering together. If it is without a path or a unifying straightness, it is shurud (wandering off) and dar-sha (stubbornness), that is, obstinacy, and it entails dispersal. Ibn Faris said: "Shareda al-ba'ir shurudan (the camel bolted away), and I shareadtu bihi tashridan (I made it bolt)." As for His saying ﴿then scatter those behind them﴾, the meaning is: punish them and make them a warning. (p-311) Al-Qazzaz said: "Sharradtu al-rajul tashridan" means I drove the man away, and "sharradtu bihi" means I made him notorious and mentioned his faults to the people. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then scatter those behind them﴾ means: make them fugitives. End of quotation.

So the meaning is: exaggerate in striking them, for when they are struck with a blow they scatter in disorder and without order. Those behind them, learning that terror has reached them, become terrified themselves, and so fall into flight, either in potential or in actuality. According to the reading that makes "min" (from) a preposition, the object is omitted, and the sense is: strike, by what you do to these men of terrifying affairs, a scattering in the place behind them, through the flight of those in it, either in potential or in actuality, because of what they heard or saw of the state of these men when they confronted you for battle. According to the reading that makes it a relative noun, it is the object, so the meaning is: scatter those behind them from their places, either actually or potentially, such that their hearts are divided by what you do to these men, and they become, seeing their wretched state, prone to flight. The difference in meaning lies between partitive sense when "min" is a preposition and generality when it is a relative pronoun, regarding potency or action.

When He mentioned the ruling, He mentioned its fruit with the particle of hope, bringing it back to hope, saying: ﴿so that they may take heed﴾, that is, the scattered and those by whom they are scattered, ﴿may be mindful﴾ of the past days of Allah, so that they know that these are His deeds and these are His men, and that this benefits them, so they do not break a covenant after it. The Prophet (ﷺ) did this to them: if they were the Banu Qurayzah, he (ﷺ) struck them with a blow from which no informant escaped. Rather, he struck their necks in trenches in the market of Madinah, and they were about seven hundred, all under one blood-claim, except those among them who converted to Islam, and they were few. He took their children and women captive and seized their wealth. If they were Qaynuqa', he descended upon their courtyard after their breaking of the covenant and their open display of extreme contempt and obstinacy, and Allah did not humble them to the point of placing them in His grasp, and nothing remained but striking their necks, as happened to the Banu Qurayzah. Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, the hypocrite, interceded for them, pressing him (ﷺ) insistently in their matter, for he had an intimate bond with him and was won over by him, so he (ﷺ) left them for him and expelled them from Madinah. Their incident was the first of the Jewish incidents in Madinah. If they were the Banu al-Nadir, they too had broken the covenant, so he surrounded them, and the hypocrites deceived them with false promises, so Allah cast terror into their hearts, and they asked him (ﷺ) to expel them and spare their blood, and he did. Then Allah completed the matter for him regarding them at Khaybar, Wadi al-Qura, and elsewhere, until He left none of them in the Arabian Peninsula without striking them with humiliation and imposing abasement and disgrace upon them. His campaigns against them are well known in report and recorded in the sirah (biographical literature).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 58:

When He had commanded him regarding what to do with those whose treachery was certain, He guided him to what to do with those whose treachery he feared, saying: ﴿And if you fear treachery﴾ from a people — with emphasis, indicating that the indications are manifest and the signs clear — ﴿from a people﴾, that is, people of strength, between you and whom there is a covenant, ﴿treachery﴾, that is, in that covenant, ﴿then throw back﴾, that is, cast off with the casting of one who disdains and holds in contempt, ﴿to them﴾, that is, that covenant, a casting-off ﴿on equal terms﴾, that is, a matter level in knowledge of its termination between you and them, and in justice and equity, and do not engage them in battle while they are under the assumption that the covenant still holds. This is an indication that they should be in the utmost state of caution and of searching for news of the enemy, such that they do not leave him until he breaks the covenant and then they know his inclination to breaking it and cast back his covenant to him; for that is more of a deterrent to him, and it is more conducive to peace. Then he gave the reason for the permissibility of the casting-off and the obligation of equity by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿does not love the treacherous﴾, that is, He does not treat them with the treatment of one who loves, neither from you nor from others.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 59:

Since abandoning a treaty is likely to cause fear of the enemy's increase and their awakening (to hostility), and since attack is more fitting for fear, Allah, glorified is He, followed that with what takes place in this regard and consoles (the Prophet) about the escape of those among the disbelievers who fled at the Battle of Badr, so that they were neither killed nor taken captive. He said: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose﴾ with the yā' (third person masculine, "yahsabanna") as a third-person form according to the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Hafs, meaning: none of your followers [at any] time whatsoever. The reasoning behind the reading of the rest with the second person (taḥsabanna) is that the command and prohibition of a leader have a greater impact on the souls of followers and are more conducive to their listening. ﴿Who disbelieved﴾, meaning: all of those who broke the treaty and those who did not break it. ﴿Have outstripped﴾, meaning: they gained the advantage, which is victory at some point in time; for indeed they have not escaped any of Our commands. Then He justified that with His saying: ﴿Indeed, they cannot escape﴾, meaning: [they do not] escape anything that would increase Our domination over them. That is to say: do not let their superiority, their large numbers, and the course of many matters going according to their wishes deceive you, for all of that is by Our arrangement, and nothing goes outside Our will. It is certain that We will destroy them, for they are in Our grip; they have not gotten out of it and will not get out of it, let alone escape it. So be patient.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 60:

Since this might lead to abandoning confrontation, fighting and contending, relying on the true promise confirmed by the great victory they had received at Badr despite the lack of numbers and equipment, he followed it with what shows that the necessary course is to tie causes to their effects, so that the truthful in their claim of faith is distinguished from others. He said: ﴿And prepare against them﴾, i.e., against the enemies,

﴿whatever you are able﴾, i.e., whatever enters within your obedience and is within the reach of your strength and capacity,

﴿of power﴾, whatever power it may be. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it as archery, indicating that it is the greatest of its preparations, in the manner of "the Hajj is Arafah." In his command with the words ﴿and of steeds of war﴾ there is an allusion to a kind of favour regarding the victory at Badr, because they had with them only two horses there. The ribat (steeds kept ready) are the horses that are tethered in the way of God, a fifth or more of them. He singled them out, although they are included in what came before, to indicate their great usefulness. Ribat also means constant readiness that strikes terror into the enemy, and tethering horses for it is a preparation against the enemy. Then he answered one who might seem to say: "We did not do that, and is victory anything but from Your hand?" with his words: ﴿you will strike terror﴾, i.e., you will frighten with a great and striking fear that leads to flight, as I have set up the customary ways, ﴿by it﴾, i.e., by that which I have commanded you of what is within your power or of the steeds, ﴿the enemy of God﴾, i.e., the one to whom all greatness belongs, because He is the Supreme King, ﴿and your enemy﴾, i.e., the fighters (against you). The most fitting reading of his words ﴿and others﴾, i.e., and you will terrify by that others, ﴿besides them﴾ — i.e., it is taken to mean the hypocrites, given their description in his words ﴿you do not know them﴾, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become accustomed to hypocrisy. You do not know them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 101]. And because they are not "besides them" except when they are not like them in enmity, and everyone else who is assumed not to be hypocrites openly manifests enmity, whereas the hypocrites, by displaying Islam, claim to be friends, not enemies. ﴿God﴾, i.e., the One who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, ﴿knows them﴾, i.e., He suffices you against what is feared of their affair, and nothing is incumbent upon you except striving according to what you know. The verse, in relation to what precedes it, is of the type: "Tie it and trust" (tie your camel and then trust in God). The meaning: do not think that the disbelievers have escaped us or eluded our punishment by refraining from you, for they are in our grasp wherever they turn and wherever they settle; we will destroy them and they cannot overpower us. Yet despite this, let not reliance on our power lead you to abandon the means of contending with them through the strengths We have given you; rather, exert your effort and capacity in preparing the stratagems of war and what relates to archery in terms of power, and to horses in terms of spear-thrusting, striking and horsemanship, so that by that We may cast your terror into the hearts of your enemies, near and far, those whom you know of them and those whom you do not know.

Since most of the meanings of this verse concern spending, because the foundation of preparing strength rests upon it, he encouraged it with his words: ﴿And whatever you spend in the way of God﴾, i.e., of things, even if small, ﴿will be repaid to you﴾, i.e., its reward in full, in this world and the Hereafter, repaid in the most complete manner, multiplied, at a time when you most need it, ﴿and you will not be wronged﴾.

Since what is feared is any kind of deficiency, he used the passive form in his words ﴿you will not be wronged﴾, i.e., you will not be diminished in any part of it; as for increase, it is certainly there, and it is in proportion to the intention.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 61:

Since the guarantee of victory and the oath concerning expenditure necessitate the continuance of confrontation and distance from peace, he followed it with His saying, as a directive to moderation: ﴿And if they incline﴾, i.e., they turn toward and come forward in eagerness and resolute seeking, ﴿to peace﴾, i.e., reconciliation. The use of the preposition "lam" (li-) rather than "ila" (ila) is not devoid of an allusion to eagerness for that, so that the sincerity of the inclination may be established. ﴿Then incline﴾ [to it]. Since al-silm (peace) is masculine but may be feminized, He said: ﴿to it﴾, i.e., to reconciliation. Or its feminization is by the feminization of its opposite, al-harb (war). It seems that the feminine was chosen as an indication that it is to be confined to the least possible duration according to need. This applies when the benefit to the Muslims lies in that, namely when they are in a state of weakness. The maximum period of permissibility is ten years, following the example of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so extension is not permitted.

And since this might prompt the objection that treachery has been known from them, such that I know they are naturally disposed to a state in which they cannot be trusted, so that making peace with them is a danger without benefit, he alluded to what negates that by His saying: ﴿And put your trust in Allah﴾, i.e., He who possesses all the attributes of greatness regarding what you are aware of of their treachery. For He will suffice you in their affair and will make it a cause of their destruction, as occurred in the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya, for their betrayal in it was the cause of the conquest. The preposition "ʿala" (upon) in this and similar contexts indicates that He acts with the one who trusts (in Him) as the bearer of what has been entrusted to Him, and capable of bearing it. Then he gave a reason for the command to trust, whose meaning is the absence of fear regarding the outcome of their affair in that, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is﴾, i.e., alone, ﴿the All-Hearing﴾, i.e., the one who reaches hearing fully, so He hears everything they have settled upon in that and other matters, secretly just as He hears it openly; ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, i.e., the one who reaches knowledge fully, alone, so He knows all that they concealed just as He knows what they made public.

Then he explicitly expressed contempt for their scheming, saying: ﴿And if they intend﴾ — that is, the disbelievers — ﴿to deceive you﴾ — that is, by what they bring about of peace-making or otherwise — ﴿then indeed, sufficient for you﴾ — that is, your sufficiency — ﴿is Allah﴾ — that is, the One who possesses all the attributes of might. Then he gave the reason for His sufficiency, or began to explain it, with his saying: ﴿He is the One who strengthened you with His help﴾ — that is, He alone — ﴿and with the believers﴾ — that is, afterwards, in this battle in which the custom had dictated that those with you would not stand against the disbelievers for the time it takes between two milkings of a she-camel. Perhaps this is a reminder of the situation at the beginning of Islam, meaning: He who sent you, when you were alone in Makkah among all the disbelievers and a stranger among them, even though they were your paternal cousins, because of your call to this religion and your elevation above their bestial conditions to the angelic morals, is the One who alone strengthened you with victory over them, so that they were not able to inflict any harm that would turn you back from calling to Allah, despite all of them setting up the nets of treachery against you and your followers and extending the hands of plotting toward you. Then He removed you from among them, just as a hair is pulled out of dough, despite their striving to prevent you from that. And He strengthened you with the Helpers, and united their word after severe enmity.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 63:**

﴿And He brought their hearts together﴾ after the utmost enmity, so that the distant among them became near, the hateful became beloved, and the enemy became a friend, and they were of one heart. Then he resumed the report of what shows that their union would have been impossible without Him, saying: ﴿Even if you had spent everything that is on the earth, all of it﴾, that is, while you are the most skilled of creation in what you do, ﴿you could not have brought their hearts together﴾, that is, even if you had willed that. Then he confirmed this with His words: ﴿But Allah brought them together﴾, that is, He is the one who possesses all the attributes of perfection. Then he gave the reason for the effectiveness of His act and command in this matter with His words: ﴿Indeed, He is Mighty and Wise﴾, that is, because were it not for His might, which overcomes everything and is not overcome by anything, and His wisdom, by which He perfects what He wills so that no one can change any part of it, they would not have come together, since before this each person in both groups found the other more hateful than the sweetness of life and the purity of living, because of the enmities among them that never cease to stir up and boil in the breasts until they boil over, with the killing of loved ones, parents and children, and the subjugation through all kinds of harm, along with (p-319) the proximity that necessitates the continuation of envy and the arousing of grudges. And likewise He, glorified is He, did with all the Arabs after the widespread killing that had existed among them, together with the zealotry and pride that carry them to revenge.

The One who supplied you with these kindnesses is living and does not die, remaining as He was in power and might. So He is the guarantor of your protection from whoever wants to deceive you. Therefore, when He commands you to something, obey Him without pondering its outcome, for He has made it clear by His might and perfected it by His wisdom. ﴿And you will surely know﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 64:

When he had declared explicitly that Allah is sufficient for him, and the sufficiency of Allah for the servant is the greatest of aims, the souls turned to the question of whether He suffices him absolutely, or whether He also did the same for the believers. So He followed it with His saying, describing him with the attribute of prophethood (nubuwwah), whose meaning is elevation and being informed by Allah of what the servants do not know, because it is in the context of informing about some of the unseen matters and of disposing of the malakut (the invisible dominion):

﴿O Prophet﴾, that is, the one of high rank whom We inform of the outcomes of his affairs. ﴿Sufficient for you﴾, that is, sufficient for you is ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the One in whose hand is everything. ﴿And those﴾, that is, together with those ﴿who follow you among the believers﴾. The word "with" (ma'iyyah) may be understood as referring to his pronoun (ﷺ), so that the believers are the ones being sufficed; or it may be understood as referring to the Name of Majesty (al-Jalalah), so that they are the ones who suffice; until the meaning becomes: He is sufficient for them as well, and they are sufficient for you, because He is with them. Glorified is He, He stated this in this manner to comfort their hearts and console their spirits. And according to the second meaning, because it includes the first and adds to it. Ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi said: (p-320) "Allah is sufficient for you, and those who follow you are sufficient for you." He stated it in a repeated form to show the sufficiency of His Prophet (ﷺ), it being possible that among those who followed him at that time there was sufficiency, so that they would not consider themselves few in comparison to the multitude of their enemies.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 65:

When he had shown that they were sufficient and made sufficient for, and that this was conditional upon acting with astuteness and resolve, which is striving according to one's capacity, He commanded him to urge them to that by which they would be sufficient: earnestness in fighting and not fearing the brave in any circumstance. So He said, expressing it with the attribute that looks toward the source of the receiving from Allah, so that the listener's confidence in what he hears may be strengthened: ﴿O Prophet﴾, that is, the one elevated in station with Us, the one granted from Our information everything that gladdens his eye and the eyes of his followers, ﴿urge the believers﴾, that is, those immersed in faith, ﴿to fighting﴾, that is: exert yourself in urging them to it and in exhorting them to it by every means.

The root ḥ-r-ḍ, in whatever order it occurs — ḥ-r-ḍ, ḥ-ḍ-r, r-ḥ-ḍ, r-ḍ-ḥ, ḍ-r-ḥ — returns to presence (ḥuḍūr). It entails ease and repose, and it entails idleness, and idleness entails weakness, and weakness entails corruption. From it comes ḥaraḍ (the one who has come close to destruction), that is, his destruction has become present and he himself has become present in the place where he is, so that he is bound to that condition as long as he lives. And raḥaḍa the garment means he washed it, from repose (daʿah), which is the condition of those present, not travellers. Ruḥāʾ (rahaḍāʾ) is the sweat of fever, a metaphor for something washed. Miraḍ (al-mirḍāḥ) is the stone that is always present for crushing the date-stone. Ḍarīḥ is a long cleft in which the dead person is placed, so that its presence is necessarily constant for him until the known time. It also entails throwing and length. From it comes maḍraḥī, for the falcon with long wings, because every prey is present to it by the strength of its flight; and for the noble man, for the loftiness of his resolve. And "the mount was brought (uḥḍirat al-dābba)" means it was readied, so it made the absent present. And taḥrīḍ is urging toward the presence of a thing, so "ḥarriḍ ʿalā al-qitāl" means: urge toward flying to it by pursuing its means and preparing for its presence, until the one urged becomes as if present. When one says "yā ṣabāḥāh!" he flies to the caller, and is the first to be present at the gathering, because nothing prevents him from anything, but his readiness is the readiness of one present in the row.

The Imam Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā al-Rummānī said in his tafsir: "Taḥrīḍ is an emphatic call to move the soul toward a matter of affairs; ḥathth, taḥrīḍ and taḥḍīḍ are synonyms, and its opposite is tafsīr. Taḥrīḍ is encouragement toward an action with what provokes hastening toward it, together with patience in it." End of quotation.

This is its true meaning, not what was said in the Kashshāf and followed by al-Bayḍāwī upon it.

When He had urged them to fighting, He informed them that they would be victorious in it if they persisted in the means of victory. So He said, resuming as an answer to one who asks: what will be their outcome if they desire it and hasten to it? ﴿If there are among you twenty﴾ — and since the pleasure of direct address stirs resolves, arouses determinations and necessitates complete confidence in the promise, He turned from the third person to say: ﴿among you twenty﴾, that is, men, ﴿steadfast﴾, that is, in the steadfastness mentioned before, ﴿they will overcome two hundred﴾, that is, of the unbelievers. The verse is among the true promises which the battles of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, fulfilled. ﴿And if there are among you a hundred﴾, that is, steadfast, ﴿they will overcome a thousand﴾, that is, of those who disbelieved. The verse is of iḥtibāk (the rhetorical device of mutual omission): it mentioned in the first the attribute of steadfastness as evidence of its omission in the second, and in the second it mentioned disbelief as evidence of its omission in the first. Perhaps what He made obligatory upon them of this steadfastness is the reason for the command to urge: that is, urge them, for I have aided each of them against ten, so there is no excuse for them in slackness. He explained their superiority over them and their overcoming of them on this basis with His saying: ﴿because they are a people who do not understand﴾, that is, what I have made obligatory and in whose support I promised victory is because of this: that the unbelievers are a people who have no understanding by which they know the knowledge of war which the people of faith have trained in, even if you see them as strong in bodies, having sufficiency among them to carry out what befalls them of worldly affairs, because they are bodies without meanings, just as the world is likewise a form without spirit. For they did not build their confrontation upon those five pillars which I presented to you and inspired in you at Badr. Whoever does not gather them does not understand war, for if an army has no leader to whom it returns, it does not prosper; and if that leader's command is not resting upon the King of kings, his heart is weak and his resolve, even if his hosts are numerous, is unsteady, for they become forms without meanings, and forms are acted upon, not acting, while meanings are the ones that act. One who relies upon Allah has his form joined with meaning. So the least that is required, in facing two of his enemies, is as He set down the matter (p-323) in jihad. Perhaps this is the secret of the victory of the Khawārij — followers of Shabīb and his likes — despite their small number, over the armies they used to meet from the kings of their time despite their multitude. For the Khawārij believe their fighting is for Allah, relying in this belief upon the injustice of those kings and their departure from the command of Allah. Those they met on behalf of those kings, though they believed them to be people of obedience, obeying the imam whose obedience is obligatory, nonetheless know that their imam's reliance upon Allah is weak because he opposes the path of uprightness; and that leader himself believes this, and that his rule is corruption, and that the Prophet's ﷺ prohibition of fighting him was only to avert the greater of the two evils. Thus the reliance of the Khawārij upon the King of kings became greater than the reliance of those others. For this reason, from the Khawārij's reliance arose asceticism, which is the greatest cause of victory, and from the reliance of those kings arose inclination toward the world, which is the greatest cause of abandonment. The proof of this is that when they rebelled against ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, he proceeded among them according to Allah's sunnah of gentleness toward them, presenting admonition to them, giving them excuse, and returning them to Allah. When they did not accept his intention at one hour, one of those who cared for the stars said to him: "It is an hour of misfortune; if he marches in it, he will be forsaken." He said: "March in it, for the Prophet ﷺ had no astrologers." When he met the Khawārij, they did not stand against him the time it takes to milk a she-camel, nor did any of them escape, nor was any man of his company killed.

And the obligation was understood from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If there are among you twenty﴾ — the verse — and that the report in it carries the meaning of a command, from His saying:

[p. 324] **"Now Allah has lightened [the burden] from you"** (﴿الآنَ خَفَّفَ اللَّهُ عَنْكُمْ﴾): that is, the King, to whom belongs absolute self-sufficiency and all attributes of perfection. **"from you"** means out of mercy toward you and gentleness with you. **"And He knew"** means that before the lightening He knew His promise, **"that there is weakness in you"** means in number and in equipment. But He had made that obligation upon you as a trial. So after the lightening, He knew your weakness as an actual fact, and before it He knew that it would occur. Opening this sentence with **"Now"** (﴿الآنَ﴾) indicates that the abrogation (naskh, the replacement or cancellation of a ruling by a later one) took place before a period had passed in which a military campaign could have been carried out. The benefit of a command that is followed by abrogation is that one gains reward by accepting it and by resolving to carry it out. It has also been said that the abrogation came only after a period of time had passed, after they had asked for lightening. Al-Bukhari narrated in the Book of Tafsir, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: When the verse ﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 65] was revealed, it was hard on the Muslims, since it had been made obligatory on them that not one of them should flee from ten [of the enemy]. Then the lightening came, and He said: ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] from you﴾, to the end of the verse. When Allah lightened the number [required] from them, the steadfastness demanded of them was reduced by the same measure as the lightening.

The meaning is that He had prescribed a certain measure of steadfastness for every believer, and when He lightened it, He removed that [prescription] with respect to the group as a whole. This does not prevent some of them from continuing in what was prescribed, as He did with the Companions, may Allah's good pleasure be upon them, on more than one occasion, including the battle of Mu'tah. In it they were three thousand, and the forces of Heraclius that they met numbered two hundred thousand: one hundred thousand Romans and one hundred thousand Arabs who had been enlisted as allies. They stood firm against them and were given victory over them, as is found in the Sahih, where the Prophet ﷺ said, reporting about them in this campaign: "Then the banner was taken, without a command, by a sword of the swords of Allah, Khalid ibn al-Walid, and Allah granted him victory." When the Prophet ﷺ died, most of the people apostatized [p. 325] until only one-tenth of one-tenth remained firm in Islam. The Companions, may Allah's good pleasure be upon them, stood firm against them and were given victory over them. Indeed, the one who in reality stood firm was Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, alone. Then Allah bestowed upon all the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, of his steadfastness and his light, and they stood firm. Then he equipped the army, and its commander was the one whom the Prophet ﷺ named "the Sword of Allah." By him Allah extinguished the fire of polytheism, and by his steadfastness and good intention he cut off the roots of disbelief. Within a year there was not a single polytheist left in the lands of the Arabs.

When Allah united the Arabs under this religion, upon the heart of one man, they set out against the non-Arabs: the Persians, the Romans, and the Copts. They fought the people of Persia in a number of battles, among them al-Qadisiyyah. The Companions in it were fewer than forty thousand, while the Magians were more than four hundred thousand. They likewise fought the Romans, and at al-Yarmuk they were fewer than forty thousand, while the Romans were about four hundred thousand, and there were other battles besides these. They stood firm in most of them and were given victory. Then the final outcome was theirs, and they drove out polytheism and its people, and Allah made His religion manifest for them, as He had promised, glorified is He. Never did the people of Islam and the people of error meet in a battlefield without the dead of the disbelievers being many times the dead of the Muslims. Yet Allah, exalted is His majesty, blessed is His name, and fulfilled is His word, showed greater kindness to the Arabs, knowing that they are the elite of mankind, because of the praiseworthy qualities and upright characters with which He had formed them. So everyone whom their peninsula encompassed embraced Islam after a series of battles in the time of the Prophet ﷺ and in the time of the apostasy. Their dead, as far as I think, did not reach ten thousand people. Then, [p. 326] when they fought the non-Arabs from Persia, Rome, and others, the dead of the disbelievers in a single battle reached one hundred thousand and two hundred thousand, as is well known in the books of conquests by al-Madā'inī, Sayf, Ibn Abd al-Hakam, al-Baladhuri, and others. Al-Hafiz Abu al-Rabi' ibn Salim al-Kala'i and his teacher Ibn Hubaysh collected the scattered reports of that. Perhaps in the second [calculation] he omitted the restriction to "disbelievers," so as to include everyone who deserved to be fought, such as rebels and others. Then, Allah, exalted, said, giving the reason for the aforementioned lightening, and turning the command from obligating steadfastness against ten to a command of steadfastness against double [the enemy's number]: if the enemy's number exceeds double, fleeing is permitted, though steadfastness is better: **"So if there are among you one hundred steadfast"** that is, the steadfastness that has already been pointed out, **"they will overcome two hundred"** that is, of others than you, **"by Allah's permission."** **"And if there are among you a thousand"** that is, with the aforementioned attribute, which is steadfastness, **"they will overcome two thousand."** Then He guided to the fact that the meaning of steadfastness is everything commanded in the verse: ﴿When you meet a force, stand firm﴾ [al-Anfal: 45]. So He said: **"by Allah's permission,"** that is, by the will of the One to whom all command belongs, and by His authorization and enablement for you. If permission does not occur, victory does not occur. So the verse is of the kind called *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which one element is mentioned and its counterpart is omitted, and the omitted element is understood from the mentioned one): he mentioned "steadfast" in the first clause as an indication of its omission in the second, and he mentioned "permission" in the second as an indication of its omission in the first. Then he drew attention to the generality of the ruling by his words: **"And Allah is with the steadfast"** that is, the One encompassing all attributes of perfection, **"with His help and support."** For this reason Ibn Shubrumah said: "I see that enjoining good and forbidding evil is likewise."

The root of *idhan* (إذن) is hamzated, unhamzated, waw-based, and ya-based, with its four permutations: *idhan*, *dhan*, *dhawan*, *dhayan*. [p. 327] It goes back to knowledge arising from the sense of hearing, connected with the organ of the ear. Sometimes it produces permission and sometimes prohibition. *Adhina bi-l-shay'* (أذن بالشيء), like *sami'a*, means: he came to know it. ﴿فَأْذَنُوا بِحَرْبٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279], that is: be aware that your war has been permitted. *Adhina lahu bi-l-shay'* (أذن له بالشيء), likewise like *sami'a*, means: he permitted it for him. *Ādhanahu al-amr wa-bihi* (آذنه الأمر وبه) means: he informed him of it, both in form and in meaning, so he made it permitted for him or forbidden to him. *Adhana fulānan ta'dhīnan* (أذن فلانا تأذينا) means: he twisted his ear. *Adhanahu* (أذنه) means: he turned him back from drinking so that he did not let him drink, as if the intensive form here indicates removal. *Ādhana al-na'l wa-ghayrahā* (آذن النعل وغيرها) means: he made an ear for it. *Fa'alahu bi-idhnī* (فعله بإذني) means: with my knowledge and my enablement. *Adhina ilayhi wa-lahu*, like *fariḥa* (أذن إليه ولهُ كفرح), means: he listened with his ear, that is, that permitted his hearing and his heart. *Adhina li-rā'ihat al-ta'ām* (أذن لرائحة الطعام) means: he desired it, as if he had permitted it to himself. *Ādhanahu īdhānan* (آذنه إيذانا) means: it pleased him, the same in meaning. *Ādhanahu* also means: he forbade him, as if the *hamza* there indicates removal. *Al-udhun* (الأذن) is the well-known organ, with a single or double *damma*. Also *al-miqbid* (the handle) and *al-urwa* (the grip) of anything, and of a mountain, because each of these is a means of being enabled to carry what is in it. *Al-udhun* also means a man who listens and accepts everything said to him, as if, when he accepted it, he permitted it into his heart and enabled it. *Al-adhān* (الأذان) is the call to prayer, because it is an announcement of its permissibility and of the ability to perform it. *Ta'adhdhana* (تأذن) means: he swore and he informed. Sometimes it results in permission and enablement with respect to a thing, and sometimes in prohibition and prohibition. In this case it is from the sense of removal. *Adhana al-'ushb* (آذن العشب) means: the grass began to dry, so some of it was moist and some dry, as if it had become possible to cut and gather it when it reached its ripeness. *Al-ādhin* (الآذن) means: the chamberlain, because he is for enabling and for prohibiting. *Al-udhunah*, with a vowel on the first and second letters, means: young camels and sheep, as if they permit anyone to take from them what he wants. *Ta'ām lā udhunata lahu* (طعام لا أذنة له) means: a food with no appeal to its smell, so it is as if it [p. 328] is forbidden because it is not desired. *Ta'adhdhana al-amīr fī al-nās* (تأذن الأمير في الناس) means: the ruler proclaimed among the people with a threat, so this goes back to prohibition and deterrence from something as a discretionary punishment. *Al-dhīn* (الذين), with a *kasra* and a *ya*, means: grapes. Likewise *al-dhān* (الذان), with an *alif* that is converted from a *waw*, means: grapes. As if, because of its ease of consumption and the pleasure of its taste, one could take it readily. *Al-tadhawwun* (التذون), with a doubled *waw*, means: wealth and blessing, as if these two were a means of attaining what is desired. *Al-dhu'nūn* (الذؤنون), hamzated, like *zunbūr*, means: a plant among the plants of the earth. The meaning is that He only permitted this for you when you fulfill the aforementioned condition, because you have understood war and built your affair upon its five pillars, whose foundation and whose inner component in each is steadfastness. So Allah was with you, and He is with every steadfast person who maintains this steadfastness established in the five pillars at every time.

One question asked about this verse is that it begins with the second of the tens in the tens, and in the hundreds and thousands it begins with the first. I asked our shaykh, the firmly grounded imam, the verifier of his age, Shams al-Din Muhammad ibn Ali al-Qayati, judge of the Shafi'is in the land of Egypt, about its wisdom. He said: The original practice is to begin with the first of the tens. But if it had been said, "If there are among you ten steadfast, they will overcome a hundred," it might have been supposed that the steadfastness of one against ten is obligatory only when the believers reach this number. So He shifted to beginning with the second of the tens of this rank in order to remove this concern. When that was removed and it became known that it is obligatory for each one to stand firm against ten, He mentioned the remaining ranks in the remainder according to the customary sequence. As for the repetition of one meaning, namely the resistance of a group against more than its number, twice, before the lightening and after it, this is for the purpose of indicating, as al-Zamakhshari said in the *Kashshaf*, that the situation is one and the same whether the number is small or large, without any difference, even though one might suppose a difference. It seems that He did not mention the single units as glad tidings of the great number of this community and its unity, and He began with the tens and concluded with the thousands, in order to complete the ranks of the original numbers. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 67:

When the command to inflict thorough slaughter (al-ithkhan) was given in ﴿So scatter those behind them﴾ [al-Anfal: 57], then the preparation of strength, then the urging to fight after the announcement of sufficiency, then the obligation that one be steadfast against ten, then the lightening of this to two, that was indicative of persisting in thorough slaughter. Therefore the rebuke of the beloved ones for choosing other than what this address conveyed was apt, because that is more fitting for bestowing favour upon them with pardon and forgiveness, on account of the fact that most of them inclined toward ransoming the captives. "The Prophet ﷺ consulted them about them, and Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) advised ransom, and most of them inclined with him. And ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) advised cutting off their necks. And it is narrated that he ﷺ said: 'Had a punishment descended from the sky—i.e., over this—none would have been saved from it except ʿUmar and Saʿd ibn Muʿadh (may Allah be pleased with both of them).'" Then Allah the Exalted said, as a resumption and a deduction: ﴿It is not for a prophet﴾, i.e., it is not correct nor proper ﴿for a prophet﴾, i.e., under the law of any prophet, whether independent or confirmed. Perhaps He expressed it with the attribute of prophethood (p-330) in order to convey, together with generality, that both the elevation of rank and the information from Allah prevent proceeding to an action without specific permission ﴿that he should have captives﴾, i.e., that taking enemies captive be permitted for him ﴿until he inflicts thorough slaughter in the land﴾, i.e., he exaggerates in killing his enemies. So this is a rebuke to those among the Companions who took captives other than those whom the Prophet ﷺ had forbidden to be killed among the polytheists, or who approved of that. It was attributed to "a prophet"—and it was read irregularly with the definite article—and it did not say "under the law of a prophet," in order to magnify the taking of captives and to exalt pardon, for the sake of exaggerating in the performance of gratitude. This occurred on the day of Badr, when the Muslims were few at that time. Then when they multiplied and their authority grew strong, Allah, glorified and exalted, sent down: ﴿Then either grace afterward or ransom﴾ [Muhammad: 4]. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them). The root thakhn revolves around bulkiness; sometimes it entails softness and weakness, and sometimes firmness and strength. Its essential meaning is: he exaggerates in killing, so his affair becomes thick and grows strong, and his enemies become submissive to him and weakened. Then He explained to them that the inclination away from this is only for the desire of worldly goods, with which the Jews were rebuked at the end of the preceding verse by His saying: ﴿They take the goods of this lowly world﴾ [al-A'raf: 169]. Just as the dispute over the spoils is an inclination toward this world, and all of this is far removed from the lofty qualities of character and noble dispositions, giving as the reason for the aforementioned not being the case something whose implied sense is: because taking captives is only intended for worldly gain. This is how the underlying meaning runs, but it was expressed in the mode of direct address because it strikes the soul more forcefully, so He said: ﴿You desire﴾, i.e., you believers, who are eager to spend rather than to accumulate, by sparing them ﴿the goods of this world﴾. Al-Raghib said: "ʿaradh (goods) is that which has no permanence, and from it the theologians borrowed it for what has no permanence except through a substance, such as color." Ibn Hisham said in Tahdhib al-Sira: i.e., the provision of ransom by taking the men ﴿And Allah﴾, i.e., the One to whom all perfection belongs, ﴿desires﴾, i.e., for you, ﴿the Hereafter﴾, i.e., its essence, because He commands that by a command which, in its emphasis, is meant to be obeyed like a will whose desire is never frustrated. This is through thorough slaughter of them, for the manifestation of the religion which you wish to make manifest and by which the Hereafter is attained. It is not fitting for a lover to wish except what his beloved wishes. ﴿And Allah﴾, i.e., the Supreme King, ﴿is Mighty﴾, i.e., His lofty presence is exalted above the approach of anything in which there is the least lowness. ﴿Wise﴾, i.e., nothing proceeds from Him except that it is in the utmost perfection. So He commands thorough slaughter when the strength of the polytheists is manifest; when it weakens and the Muslims grow strong, then you have the choice.
