And the claim of His guardianship is not valid except for one who has ascended the stages of His attributes: that he be mighty in himself, so he does not defile it with fleeting desires, and mighty in his action, so he does not lower it from the summit of lofty things to the abyss of ruin; and wise, so that no action proceeds from him except that it is in the utmost perfection.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 68:

When what I have pointed to from the verse became known, it was as if they had said, "May Allah be pleased with them": "Does His might and wisdom, glory be to Him, require purifying us from what we have been defiled with?" God, exalted is He, began His answer to this, bestowing the utmost favor and warning against exposure to the places of loss, saying: ﴿Had it not been for a decree﴾, that is, a firm, settled, and binding decree, ﴿from Allah﴾, that is, the One who has complete encompassing of everything in power and knowledge, ﴿that had already preceded﴾, that is, in the Mother of the Book, concerning the judgment of your felicity, and that He would not punish anyone except after sending a prior prohibition to him, and that He would make lawful to you the ransom and the spoils which had been forbidden to those before you, as an honor to you, as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said, ﴿you would have been touched for what you took﴾, that is, of the captives, by which is meant the ransom, ﴿by a great punishment﴾. But My judgment had already preceded that the spoils, even through ransom, are lawful for you, even though you hastened in it before My command.

Having followed this glad tiding with a warning, He, glorified is He, made the following a consequence of it: ﴿So eat of what you have taken as spoils, lawful and good﴾. That is, from the ransom and other things, being ﴿lawful﴾, meaning there is no reckoning and no consequence for it from My side, ﴿good﴾, meaning wholesome and agreeable to your natures. This holds when the conditions I have set for you are met, namely not embezzling or betraying in any way, not monopolizing, and not being overcome by a strong desire that drives one to what is unseemly, such as dispute and the like. These are the matters I have already communicated to you. ﴿And fear Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses all attributes of perfection in all of this, so do not embezzle, do not dispute, and do not advance except in what the Messenger ﷺ permits you. ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One characterized by majesty and generosity, ﴿is Forgiving﴾, that is, toward whoever He knows in his heart to be among the people of taqwa (God-consciousness), ﴿Merciful﴾, that is, toward him. Because of the good He knew in your hearts, He forgave you, and did not punish you for your haste in taking captives for ransom, without the Messenger ﷺ having commanded you to ransom them and without waiting for his permission; and He showed you mercy and was gracious to you by making the spoils lawful for you. (p-333) Consider His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion and will remove from you your misdeeds and forgive you﴾ [al-Anfal: 29]; you will recognize the fine rationale of linking the command to fear Allah with forgiveness and mercy. It is also possible that this is a cause for the eating, meaning: eat, for Allah has indeed forgiven you what He reproached you for. The benefit of commanding taqwa is warning against returning to it relying on the vastness of His forbearance. Also, since a threat and a forgiveness had both preceded, it was fitting to indicate to them that the cause of forgiveness is taqwa. The summary of this is that when He instilled fear of the punishment touching them upon taking the ransom, had it not been for the prior decree of the Book, He then encouraged them: whenever a sin-driven turning away keeps them from His presence, a feeling of taqwa turns them back to Him, and He lets the hem of forgiveness and mercy fall over them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 70:

When it became known from this that it is permissible to take ransom (fida') from the captives (al-asra), and what is taken from them would be a great hardship for them, He turned to them, appealing to their sympathy and encouraging them towards Islam. So He turned to His Prophet ﷺ with the command to address them, as an alert that they are not fit to be addressed by Him, glory be to Him, because of how they distanced themselves from Him by choosing to be in the company of the enemies over being counted among the allies. So He said, using the descriptive title that looks toward receiving knowledge, to encourage receiving it from him (ﷺ): ﴿O Prophet﴾, that is: the one to whom I convey every sublime meaning, who makes His religion manifest and purifies His community, along with raising his rank and perfecting his lights. ﴿Say to those in your hands﴾, that is: in the hands of your companions and the people of your religion, since the lesson is in the generality of the wording, not in the specificity of the cause, ﴿of the captives﴾, encouraging them toward what is with Allah. ﴿If Allah knows﴾ with what He has of the attributes of majesty and beauty ﴿in your hearts any good﴾, that is: any portion of His piety that carries you to faith, which is the head of all good and the source of every good. ﴿He will give you better than what was taken from you﴾, that is: better than what He will open for you of spoils in this world and store up for you of reward in the Hereafter. ﴿And He will forgive you﴾, that is: what has passed of your sins. ﴿And Allah﴾, that is: He in whose hand is all things, ﴿is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, that is: it is of His nature to do so. The meaning, according to what is known from the story of al-'Abbas that comes below, may he be pleased with him, is that He, glory be to Him, deals with you and the likes of you, beyond what His army takes from you, with generosity. As for Him ruling to drop the ransom from you and commanding them to leave it and release you freely, based on what He knows of good and faith in your hearts that you were concealing, do not hope for that, because that would open the door to false claims, which prevent spoils and weaken the religion. The memorizer (al-Hafiz) Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in his Sirah: Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "Al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, was among the captives, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'Ransom yourself and your two nephews 'Aqil and Nawfal, and I will release you, for you are a man of wealth.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah! I was truly a Muslim, but the people compelled me.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Allah knows your Islam. If what you say is true, Allah will reward you for it. But as for the outward of your matter, it was against us.' He said: 'I have no wealth.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'Where is the wealth you deposited with Umm al-Fadl when you set out, with no one else present? Then you said: If I am struck on this journey of mine, then give al-Fadl such-and-such and 'Abd Allah such-and-such!' He said: 'By the One who sent you with the truth! No one knew of this except me and her.' So he ransomed himself with a hundred uqiyyah, and each of the others with forty uqiyyah, and he said: 'You left me to beg of the people.' He embraced Islam, and he commanded 'Aqil, and he embraced Islam. None of the captives embraced Islam besides these two."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 71:

Since the implied sense is: "If they are truthful to you and accept the glad tidings of God, He fulfils them for them," he followed it with His saying: ﴿And if they intend﴾, i.e., the captives and the disbelievers, all of them or one of them, such as Abu 'Izzah, ﴿treachery against you﴾, i.e., while you are the highest of creation in a covenant of Islam or of other than Islam, which they bind for you, and you are content with it by granting freedom to one of them without ransom. God forbid that the consequence of that should return to them, so that He enables you over them. So do not fear their affair. ﴿Then they have betrayed God﴾, i.e., the Greatest King. Since their treachery was not all-encompassing in time, he brought in the preposition, saying ﴿before﴾, i.e., before this time, with disbelief and other kinds of corruption. ﴿So He gave power﴾, i.e., He created the ability over them, and He restricted it to indicate that they had become prey for everyone ﴿over them﴾, i.e., on the Day of Badr, because of their treachery. So the empowerment at the occurrence of treachery is an example of what He will empower you over them when they intend treachery, for God knows what they conceal and what they reveal. ﴿And God﴾, i.e., the One who encompasses everything, ﴿is All-Knowing﴾, i.e., of absolute and complete knowledge, so He knows all things, including their states (p-336), ﴿All-Wise﴾, i.e., of complete wisdom, so He carries out whatever He wills. He weakens their plot and perfects what He sets against them, so it overtakes them without doubt.

"And thus did He, glory be to Him, act with Abu 'Izzah al-Jumahi. He asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to grant him freedom without anything in return, because of his poverty and his dependants, and he pledged to him that he would not support anyone against him, and he praised him. Then he betrayed, and he was exposed through him as a captive in the expedition of Hamra' al-Asad after the Day of Uhud. He made excuses to him and asked him to pardon him, and he said: 'Would that you wipe my cheeks in Makkah and say: I mocked Muhammad twice. The believer is not stung from one hole twice.' He ordered him, and his neck was struck."

Abu Hayyan said regarding the treachery: it is that some of them displayed Islam and then returned to their religion.

When al-Biqa'i had explained that the good that is not known to anyone in their hearts except Allah does not benefit them in dropping the ransom, because there is no evidence for it, and everything for which there is no evidence is treated as nonexistent, since the Sharia is built on what the accountable person can know, namely the outward matters, and he concluded with the two attributes of knowledge and wisdom, he began to explain the report that conveys the nearness on which support and every good is founded. So he divided the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) into four categories. The first category combined faith, the first emigration (hijrah, migration from the land of polytheism), and jihad (striving). The second category gave shelter. The third category believed but did not emigrate. The fourth category emigrated later. He said: ﴿Indeed those who believed﴾, that is, in Allah and His Messenger, ﴿and emigrated﴾, that is, undertook the emigration (p-337) from the lands of polytheism. These are the first emigrants. They left their homelands, their tribes, and their loved ones out of love for Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿And strove﴾, that is, undertook jihad, which is the exertion of effort in weakening disbelief and its people.

When the preceding verses concerned the instruments of jihad, namely the self and wealth, sometimes by urging spending of it, sometimes by forbidding attachment to it, and sometimes by consoling the captives for losing it, it was most fitting to put first His saying: ﴿with their wealth﴾, that is, by spending it in jihad and by losing some of it through emigration from homes, palm groves, and other things, ﴿and their lives﴾, by advancing into fighting despite the severity and multitude of the enemies. He put wealth first because it is the cause of the self's sustenance, and it was in its utmost honor at the beginning of the matter. He placed His saying ﴿in the way of Allah﴾ later, that is, the Sovereign, the Greatest, for that. The particle "fi" (in) here indicates causation, meaning they strove because of Him, so that no obstacle would turn them from Him, so that His excellences would become apparent and passage on the path would be easy without any interruption. Perhaps He expressed it with "fi" to inform that one should be firmly established on the path as a contained thing is firmly within its container, so that religion dominates him and he does not leave it in any way. As for Surah Bara'ah (Surah al-Tawbah), since its context in some places concerned the path, the path was put first, as will come. Also, this surah was revealed at the beginning of the matter after the Battle of Badr in the second year of the Hijrah, and the situation at that time was extremely severe, the wealth was extremely scarce, and the enemies were countless. So concern for wealth and self was appropriate, and both were placed first as encouragement to give them up. As for Bara'ah, it was revealed during the expedition to Tabuk at the end of the ninth year. Wealth had then become abundant, religion had become mighty, grown large, strong, and great, and most people had embraced Islam. So the places of jihad became distant, the hardship became great, people relied on one another, and they desired to focus on improving their wealth. Therefore it was fitting there to begin with the path.

When He mentioned the people of the first emigration, He followed them with the people of support, who are the second category of believers who lived in his time (ﷺ). He said: ﴿And those who gave shelter﴾, that is, those to whom the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, emigrated, so they housed them in their homes, shared their wealth with them, and offered to give them some of their women so they could marry them. He restricted the verb (in its form) to indicate the magnitude of their action, such that it is as if there was no shelter in existence other than what they did. Similarly is His saying: ﴿and helped﴾, that is, Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. They are the Ansar (Helpers), may Allah be pleased with them. They attained these two noble qualities, so they were at the summit of both excellences. Had it not been for their sheltering and their support, the aim would not have been accomplished. The first emigrants are above them because of their precedence in faith, which is the head of virtues, and because they bore harm from the disbelievers for a long time and were patient with separation from homelands and tribes.

He pointed to the two categories with the particle of distance, to indicate the loftiness of their rank and the honor of their goal, and said: ﴿Those﴾, that is, those of elevated rank, ﴿some of them are allies of others﴾, that is, in inheritance, not merely the nearness devoid of that. He made clear that faith, if it is not accompanied by two witnesses, namely emigration and jihad from those who were strangers to Madinah, and two witnesses, namely sheltering and support from the people of Madinah, it becomes an obstacle to absolute nearness, rather it prevents the influence of kinship from having any influence at all. So it is as if the one who believed but did not emigrate does not inherit from the one who emigrated. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. The root w-l-y in all its derivations returns to inclination, and it necessarily involves nearness and distance, and perhaps each of them gives rise to strength. The arrangement of the specific form (waliya) revolves around nearness, and among its necessary consequences is support. So the meaning is: some of them are relatives of others, and each is obligated toward the other with support and other things what a relative is obligated toward his relative. Therefore whenever a quality brings them together, it makes them partners in what it yields. So the attribute of presence in a battle means they share the spoils, because the kinds of jihad are many, and each one of them engaged in some of them. Support arises from the presence of all of them. The emigrant in origin is one who separates from the disbelievers with his heart and disavows them, and accompanies the believers with his love and sincerity, and takes them as allies. But since this may be hidden, the matter was tied to the indicator, which is the dwelling, because it is an apparent matter. So the emigrant became one who distances himself from the abode of the polytheists, fleeing with his religion. Then after the Hijrah of the Prophet (ﷺ), the condition for this became that the relocation be to the abode of his emigration, the blessed city of Madinah. This is the ruling for every emigrant, except those from Khuza'ah. The Prophet (ﷺ) knew of their believers and disbelievers their love for him, their sincere counsel, and their hatred of his enemy, so he did not obligate their believer to relocate. The Hafiz Abu 'Umar Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in the book al-Madkhal ila al-Istnow'ab (p-340): It is said that Khuza'ah are the allies of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because they are allies of Banu Hashim, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) included them in the treaty of the year of al-Hudaybiyyah... until he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) gave them a station that he gave to no one among the people, by making them emigrants in their own land, and he wrote for them a document to that effect. End of quote.

And their poet Nujayd ibn 'Imran al-Khuza'i said, boasting of this and of what Allah granted them through the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and other things:
Allah has brought forth clouds through our support, a heap of heavy, layered clouds.
Our emigration is in our land, and with it there is a document that came from the best sender and writer.
And for our sake a sanctity was established in Makkah, that we might seek vengeance with sharp swords.

Al-Hafiz Abu al-Rabi' ibn Salim al-Kala'i mentioned this in the chapter on the Conquest from his biography. The one who first made the alliance with them was 'Abd al-Muttalib, the grandfather of the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Waqidi said at the beginning of the Conquest expedition: Khuza'ah were allies of 'Abd al-Muttalib, and the Messenger (ﷺ) was aware of that. On the day of al-Hudaybiyyah, Khuza'ah came to him with a document from 'Abd al-Muttalib, and he read it, and it said: "In Your name, O Allah. This is the alliance of 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim with Khuza'ah when he came to him, their chiefs and men of judgment, the absent among them confirming what their present one decided. Indeed between us and you is the covenant of Allah and His pledges, which is never forgotten. The hand is one and the support is one. As long as Thubayr rises and Hira' stands firm, and as long as the sea wets a tuft of wool, it shall not increase between us and you except in renewal, forever and ever, for all time." Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, read it to him, and he said: "How well I know your alliance, and you are upon what you embraced of the alliance. Every alliance that existed in the pre-Islamic era, Islam only increases it in strength. There is no alliance in Islam." Al-Waqidi said: "Aslam came to him at Ghadir al-Ashtat," and Buraydah ibn al-Husayb brought them and said: "O Messenger of Allah, these are Aslam, and this is their dwelling place. Those of them who emigrated to you have emigrated, and some of their people remained with their livestock and livelihoods." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You are emigrants wherever you are." He called al-'Ala' ibn al-Hadrami and ordered him to write a document for them, and he wrote: "This is a document from Muhammad, Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to Aslam. Whoever among them believes in Allah and testifies that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, he has believed under the security of Allah, and he has the protection of Allah and the protection of His Messenger. Our affair and your affair are one against whoever attacks us from people with injustice. The hand is one and the support is one. For the people of their desert is the same as for the people of their settled dwellings (p-342), and they are emigrants wherever they are." Al-'Ala' ibn al-Hadrami wrote it. Then Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of Allah! Buraydah ibn al-Husayb is an excellent man for his people, of great blessing upon them. We passed by him on the night we passed by, while we were emigrating to Madinah, and he embraced Islam, and whoever of his people embraced Islam with him embraced it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Buraydah is an excellent man for his people and for other than his people. O Abu Bakr, indeed the best of people is the one who defends his people as long as he does not commit sin, for indeed sin has no good in it." End of quote.

Aslam is one of four tribes of Khuza'ah. When Makkah was conquered, emigration ceased because religion became dominant and the polytheists became weak. The sincere intention indicated by jihad took the place of emigration, as he (ﷺ) said: "There is no emigration after the Conquest, but there is jihad and intention." And he (ﷺ) said: "The emigrant is one who abandons what Allah has forbidden." So if the believer cannot manifest his religion, relocation becomes obligatory upon him.

When Subhanahu wa Ta'ala had explained the matter of the one who combined the conditions, He began to explain the ruling for the one who fell short of some of them, and this is the third category. He said: ﴿And those who believed﴾, that is, whose faith became known, ﴿but did not emigrate﴾, that is, before the Conquest, but remained in their lands, ﴿you have no allegiance to them﴾. He emphasized the negation and said: ﴿of anything﴾, that is, in inheritance nor in anything else. He encouraged them toward emigration by His saying: ﴿until they emigrate﴾, that is, until they undertake emigration to the abode of polytheism and those in it. ﴿And if they seek your help﴾, that is, ask for your support, ﴿in religion﴾, that is, (p-343) because of a matter of its affairs, while they are firmly established in religion, as a contained thing is firmly within its container, ﴿then it is incumbent upon you to help﴾, that is, it is obligatory upon you to support them against the polytheists. The meaning is that they have no right over you of kinship except in seeking support in religion, for abandoning their support leads to corruption, just as their allegiance leads to corruptions. Then He made an exception to the obligation and said: ﴿except against a people﴾ who occurred and were ﴿between you and them a covenant﴾, that is, because their seeking support would place you between two corruptions: abandoning support of a believer and breaking the covenant, and the latter is the greater of the two. So the observance of the covenant was given precedence and their support was abandoned. If Allah grants them victory over the disbelievers, then that is what is intended, without you being stained by breaking a pledge. And if the disbelievers prevail, martyrdom is attained for those of your brothers who are killed, and for those who remain there is the assurance of protection, and that would be a motive for them to emigrate. As for whoever of them apostatizes, Allah will remove him, and he will harm no one but himself, and Allah is Rich and Praiseworthy. So there has occurred, as you see, the division of believers into three categories: the highest is the emigrant, next is the supporter, and the lowest is the one who remains behind and is deficient. A fourth category remains, which will come.

Abu Hayyan said: He began with the emigrants, that is, the first ones, because they are the origin of Islam and the first to respond to Allah, the Exalted. Some emigrated to Madinah, some to Abyssinia, and some to Ibn Dhi Yazan. Then they emigrated to Madinah, and they were examples for others in faith and a cause of strengthening religion. "Whoever establishes a good sunnah, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." He followed with the Ansar, because they equaled them (p-344) in faith and in jihad with self and wealth. However, He paired with emigration the sheltering and the support, and the emigrants were singled out for precedence. He mentioned a third category, those who believed but did not support, so they missed these two virtues and were deprived of allegiance until they emigrate. Then he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) established brotherhood between the emigrants and the Ansar," so an emigrant would inherit from his Ansari brother if he had no emigrant ally in Madinah, and there was no inheritance between him and his Muslim relative who was not an emigrant. Ibn Zayd said: This affair continued like that until the Conquest of Makkah. End of quote.

But what Ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned, as will come, that the ruling on that ceased with the Battle of Badr, is more fitting for the following verse at the end of the surah, along with what supports this from the verse of al-Ahzab.

Since the implied meaning is: "Allah is All-Aware of your best interests," and since souls have impulses toward supporting relatives and loved ones and opposing others secretly, and they have stratagems that can be detected, He warned against that by His saying, coordinating with this implied clause: ﴿And Allah﴾, i.e., the One who encompasses everything in knowledge and power. Since the context is to explain the interests that organize the religion and demolish whatever is other than it, and since souls—as has been previously mentioned—have states, the emphasis on knowledge of hidden things required that He place the prepositional phrase first, which indicates exclusivity—which here is a metaphor for the comprehensiveness of knowledge alone—as a warning: ﴿is All-Seeing of what you do﴾. In this there is also an encouragement to act upon what He urged, of faith, emigration, support, spending, and striving in all of that (p-345), and a warning against acting in opposition to these. And in "al-Basir" (All-Seeing) there is an indication of knowledge of whether such deeds are sincere or mixed, so there is in it additional urging toward sincerity.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 73:

When he had explained the condition for the allegiance (muwalah) of the Muslim, he explained the allegiance of the disbeliever, what is obligatory regarding debating and contending with them concerning it, and that there is no condition for it other than absolute disbelief (kufr). For although its types differ and its aspects diverge widely, it is united by enmity toward Allah and allegiance to Satan. So He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., who brought about this attribute in whatever state they were in, ﴿are allies of one another﴾, i.e., in inheritance, support, and other matters. This is a pure report that points to the prohibition for the Muslim from allying with them. As for what has passed concerning the believers, it is a command in the form and wording of a report, meaning that in each of the disbelievers there is the strength of allegiance to the other against you, and a great inclination that urges them to hasten in that, even if the enmity of some of them toward others is intense; because you are one party and they are one party, gathered by the caller of Satan through the attribute of disbelief just as the caller of the Most Merciful gathers you through the attribute of faith. Abu Hayyan said: Before the mission of the Prophet ﷺ, the People of the Book among them used to be hostile toward Quraysh and would wait for misfortunes to befall them; then after the mission of the Prophet ﷺ, they became allied with one another [and] as one hand against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, end of quote.

What he mentioned is recorded in the biographies (siyar) and well known among the people of transmitted reports (ahl al-athar). ﴿If you do not do it﴾, i.e., the like of it, from the allegiance of the believers and hostility toward the disbelievers (p-346), as the disbelievers do through mutual support and cooperation with their persons and wealth, just as they set aside the wealth of the caravan that had escaped you until they used it to fight you at Uhud. Thus it is fitting for you to be greater than them in that; for they desire by that the crumbling of their perishable worldly life, while you build your enduring hereafter, and your Caller is a Wali, Rich, while their caller is an enemy, lowly; not to mention that you should descend to the depths of disputing over spoils. ﴿There will be fitnah﴾, i.e., a great one, ﴿on earth﴾, i.e., a confusion that diverts aims from their proper directions, ﴿and great corruption﴾, i.e., arising from that fitnah. The word "kabir" (great) looks to magnitude. It was read irregularly with the letter thā' (kabīr with ثّ), in which case its greatness is then restricted to its kinds. The explanation of the corruption is that when the believer draws near to the disbeliever and the disbeliever to the believer and they support one another, or when the believers abandon mutual support among themselves, the order dissolves and each of loosening and tying becomes disordered; speech then differs, hearts drift apart, and calamities multiply. Therefore it is obligatory upon you to be one party and one hand in allegiance, and to sever ties with the disbelievers in every respect, so that your affair may stand, your life be good, and your worldly and otherworldly affairs be set right in the utmost degree. The verse encompasses everything that is called allegiance, even in inheritance, fighting the disbelievers, and defending the Muslims by commanding and forbidding. When some scholars abandoned aiding a certain group, what Allah Most High had warned of, namely fitnah and corruption, came to pass, until the matter reached what you see of the ascendancy of the corrupters and the weakness of the people of religion. So enjoining good among them is in the utmost humiliation and strangeness; the lowest of people responds to it and it finds no supporter, while that other finds many helpers against the rebuke, and the best of people in standing with the rulers and the greatest of them in love for him becomes one who is content with his blame for his action, supposing that this is compassion toward him. And Allah is the One sought for help.

When the categories of believers had been mentioned, the emigrant, the helper, and the one who stays behind, along with the rulings on their allegiance to one another, He began to explain their differences in merit, saying: ﴿Those who believed﴾, i.e., in God and what came from Him, ﴿and emigrated﴾, i.e., from the land in which there were those who opposed Him, hastening to join His Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿and strove﴾, i.e., with what was mentioned earlier, of wealth and self, or with one of the two, ﴿in the way of God﴾, i.e., the One who possesses the attributes of perfection. They exerted their utmost effort to humble their enemies, just as the enemies exerted their utmost effort to humble them. He did not mention the instrument of striving because, given that it was mentioned earlier, it is necessarily implied. ﴿And those who gave shelter﴾, i.e., to those who emigrated to them, ﴿and helped﴾, i.e., the party of God. By His saying ﴿those﴾, i.e., the first two categories specifically, He made known ﴿they are the believers truly﴾, i.e., in the true sense of faith, because they realized their faith: the emigrant by detaching himself from everything he loves of worldly affairs, and the helper by standing against all the people of disbelief through sheltering the people of God and supporting them.

When He had described them, He explained what He had bestowed upon them, saying, indicating that a human being is a locus of deficiency, so that he, however much he strives until he is among the highest rank, does not cease to commit that for which he needs forgiveness: ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, i.e., for their slips and lapses, because the constitution of the human being is based on weakness, and shortfall is inseparable from it, however much he strives. And the religion is firm, so no one will oppose it except that it overcomes him. When He mentioned their purification through forgiveness, He mentioned (p-348) their purification through mercy, saying: ﴿and provision﴾, i.e., from the spoils and other things, in this world and the Hereafter, ﴿noble﴾, i.e., without any turbidity in it in any respect, neither in its cessation, nor in its diminution, nor in any aspect of its condition.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 8, verse 75:

When he had confined true believers to those described (above), he made clear that whoever abandons what he is upon, namely residing in the abode of disbelief and sitting back from jihad, joins the general rank of those (described), even though they are higher in rank than him. So he said, mentioning the fourth category: ﴿And those who believed﴾. And since they had delayed in responding to the call of the Prophet (ﷺ) for a period, he introduced the preposition, saying: ﴿after [this]﴾, meaning: after the delay of their belief compared to the foremost (early Muslims). ﴿And emigrated﴾, meaning: joining the foremost. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that they are those who emigrated after al-Hudaybiyyah, and he said: this is the second hijrah. ﴿And struggled with you﴾, meaning: against those of the party of Satan whom you fight. ﴿Then those are of you﴾, meaning: they have what you have and are bound by what binds you, in inheritances, spoils and other matters; because the comprehensive attribute is the basis for rulings, even though their rank is later than yours, as the particle of distance (ulā'ika) implies.

When he made clear that they are of you, he made clear that whenever the attribute that yields guardianship brings them together, kinship closeness takes precedence over anything else. So he said: ﴿And those related by blood are closer to one another﴾, meaning: among the believers who are described (above), ﴿one another﴾ in inheritance and other matters, among those characterized by the guardianship of religion, free of kinship ties. ﴿In the Book of Allah﴾ (p-349), meaning: the Qur'an, or in His ruling and apportionment which the Sovereign Almighty sent down to you, in the verses of inheritance, which are restricted to the 'asabah (agnatic heirs), so they abrogated the (general) guardianship, and there is no indication of inheritance for others. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned in al-Isti'ab, in the biography of al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr, that Badr cut off the brotherhood (muwakhah) among the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), meaning that this verse abrogates the verse: "some of them are guardians of others." Then that verse becomes, at that point, an explanation of the matter of what was before the battle of Badr. This is good, and the verse in Surat al-Ahzab supports it.

Then He (glory be to Him) gave the reason for what was mentioned with something that encourages it, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, meaning: the One who possesses all attributes of perfection, ﴿of all things is Knowing﴾. So He knows that this is what the benefit revolves around and by which unity endures, just as He knew at the outset that attaching inheritance and other things to the necessary consequences of closeness of kinship is preferable to attaching them to the Islamic brotherhood, because of what that entails of increasing your few, supporting your weakness, uniting your scattered (condition), and making the brotherhood between you like the bond of lineage. As for now, the religion has planted its foot firmly, become established with its foundations and pillars, and disbelief has turned away in defeat with its helpers, retreating. So they inherit by Islam and kinship, and they sever ties with the disbelievers, draw near to and distance from (them), and withdraw from them just as they withdrew from you, and disown them just as they disowned you. Thus the end of the surah corresponds to its beginning: with turning away from worldly life, reforming relations among people, clarifying the true believers, and entrusting all deeds to the All-Knowing without objection, and with the clarification of who is an ally and who is an enemy at the beginning of Surat al-Bara'a. And Allah is the Granter of success.
